7.12      On the query of creating synergies amongst the PSEs, the Department informed the Committee that a Committee may be
constituted to monitor adherence to inter-PSU cooperation by all PSEs is one way to achieve the inter-PSU cooperation. Perhaps
amalgamations, mergers and strategic alliances could be equally effective way to bring about synergies among the PSEs and to
improve their competitive strength to become global players especially in the present competitive environment. A number of small
companies in the same discipline which if amalgamated could substantially show better operational efficiency and growth
possibilities. Therefore, a policy of mergers and amalgamations of bringing together PSEs working in the same area of activities
would improve their global competitive strength.
 
7.13      The Committee is of the view, that the very existence of several Central PSEs is at stake and if they do not bring in
synergies amongst themselves by resorting to inter-PSE cooperation, the possibility of their survival appears dim. The
Committee, therefore strongly recommends that strategic alliances may be made amongst PSEs in a mutually beneficial
manner and for that DPE should be an initiative by devising suitable mechanisms on a priority basis.  The Committee,
therefore, recommends that Department of Public Enterprises should appoint a Task Force to devise a mechanism early.
             
 
MEMORANDUM OF UNDERSTANDING (MoU)
 
8.         The New Industrial Policy, 1991 laid greater emphasis of the MoU system requiring all PSEs to be brought under the ambit of
the MoU system. With the advent of the privatization and globalisation in Indian Economy mainly after the implementation of  New
Industrial Policy, 1991, the Central PSEs have been exposed to the domestic and international competition. Now, these  PSEs  have  
to   compete  with  the    private  sector  in   the   consumer  economy. In such a stiff competitive environment, it is essential for a PSE
to have an edge of both cost and quality over its competitors. MoU system has been accepted by the PSEs as a panacea since it has
given them more freedom to take decisions independently  and operate more effectively and proficiently.
 
8.1        The MoU system is based on the principle of increased autonomy and accountability.  The commitments of the Managements

73rd Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/73rdreport.htm[04-07-2016 12:15:38]
and the Government are decided before the beginning of the financial year.  In order to achieve the targets as indicated in the MoU the
management is delegated certain financial and administrative powers to take effective decisions in their day-to-day operations.  Thus,
the PSEs have been enjoying much more autonomy while taking crucial decisions in their operations. Under the MoU system the
financial performance of the PSEs is evaluated mainly through the gross margin.
8.2        The main purpose of the MoU system are to :
 
(i)                  Measure the performance of PSEs taking into account the complexity of fusing social and financial objectives and
translating them into measurable parameters:
(ii)                Ensure simultaneous increase in autonomy as well as accountability;
(iii)               Set up new institutions and administrative & personnel systems;
(iv)              Replace `multiple principles with multiple objectives’ with clarity in goals and objectives; and
(v)                Break the vicious circle of NOT ME syndrome.
 
8.3        The main objective of the MoU system was to improve the performance of the PSEs through the mechanism of increased
autonomy and accountability and also to provide a uniform method of evaluation of the performance of the managements of the PSEs
in an objective and transparent manner. Further, it was also envisaged to provide a clarity of goals/objectives to be achieved by PSEs.
 
8.4        The objectivity, neutrality and transparency are the inbuilt features of the MoU system.  The performance of the managements
of the PSEs is evaluated with respect to the pre-determined targets and the performance evaluation reports are prepared by the PSEs
themselves at the end of the year. There is a body of experts called Ad-hoc Task Force (ATF), which is constituted every year by the
Department of Public Enterprises. The ATF acts as a third party neutral body during the MoU negotiation meetings to ensure that the
targets decided during these meetings are realistic.
 
8.5        On the recommendation of the Arjun Sengupta Committee Report, the MoU system was first implemented during the year
1987-88 with 4 PSEs signing the MoU.  For the financial year 2001-02 a total of 105  PSEs signed the MoU with their respective
Ministries.  If we take into account the subsidiaries of these MoU signing PSEs then the total number of PSEs covered under the MoU
system will work out to 163.  Every year the PSEs are shortlisted for signing the MoU and efforts are made to bring all significant
PSEs under the ambit of MoU system.  For the year 2002-03, new PSEs like Bharat Sanchar Nigam Ltd,  Konkan Railways
Corporation Limited,  Semi Conductor Complex Ltd. etc. have been shortlisted for signing the MoU.  
 
8.6        The MoU signing PSEs are delegated certain financial and administrative powers such as power to incur capital expenditure
up to Rs. 50.00 crores and Rs. 100.00  crores on replacement/renewal of assets,  freedom to finalize wage revision, transfer of
functional Directors, etc.
8.7        The Committee is happy to note that the MoU system has enabled the DPE to undertake objective assessment of CPSEs. The
Committee recommends for further strengthening of the MoU system and hopes it will be able to adopt itself to the requirements of
PSEs in a globalised economy.
 
8.8        It was informed by the Department that the Department of Public Enterprises issued the guidelines to all the Public Sector
Enterprises and the administrative Ministries emphasising that while preparing the MoUs for the year 2002-03, it should be ensured
that the MoU targets flow from the corporate/vision plan and these targets should be linked to the corporate plan of the organisation.
Sometimes, it may not be possible to exactly link the MoU targets with the corporate plan of the PSE due to fast changing economic
environment in such an eventuality the PSEs are required to indicate the reasons for any such variation. As regards coverage of more
number of PSEs under the MoU system it is clarified that at present more than 100 central PSEs are signing MoU and if the
subsidiaries are also taken into account the number of PSEs covered under the MoU will be around 163. Administratively it may not
be feasible to cover the PSEs referred to BIFR. At present only few small and insignificant PSEs are left out of the purview of MoU
system. However, this Department will continue its efforts to bring all the PSEs under the MoU system.
           
8.9        The Committee is happy to note that over 100 Central PSEs have signed the MoU. The Committee is of the view that
effects to bring more PSEs under the ambit of MoU system be made in the right earnest.
 
8.10      The Committee recommends that Department of Public Enterprises should separately submit a status note to the Committee
highlighting the benefits reaped by MoU signing P.S.Us and citing the probable reasons which presented other profit making P.S.Us
from signing MoU so as to enable the Committee  to take a more in front view on the efficacy of the system.

challenges of the dynamic situation. However, this Department has made an effort to avail the best available expertise in a cost
effective manner by availing the services of professionals, management experts and senior retired Government Officers through the
Ad-hoc Task Force (ATF). While it is true that actual achievements in bringing together the PSEs are far from satisfactory, the
Department of Public Enterprises will continue to explore further such possibilities through the MoU negotiation meetings.

2.         At the outset, Convenor welcomed the Secretaries and other officers of the ministries and representatives of industries’
associations.  Convenor apprised the committee that in its last meeting held on 16
th April 2002, discussion could not be concluded and
he requested CII to prepare a note regarding imports at zero customs duty against World Bank/Asian Development Bank’s financed
projects.  The Convenor summarised the viewpoints of CII and informed the committee that World Bank as well as Asian
Development Bank had been financing various kinds of projects for over two decades in India.  There was an established procedure
for inviting tenders and for evaluating them.  The primary features of the guidelines were as follows:-
 
(i) Evaluation of tenders submitted by foreign bidders would be evaluated without  including customs duty; and
 
(ii) Price preference of 15% to domestic bidders was allowed with the stipulation that it would be admissible if in the
total package, there was value addition of 30% or more and the price preference was not more than applicable customs duty.
 
 
3.         The Central Board of Excise and Customs Duty issued a notification No. 85/99 amending an earlier customs notification
exempting customs duty on import of goods for execution of projects financed by loan or grant by World Bank, Asian Development
Bank or any other international organisation.  The World Bank had allowed 15% Price Preference to domestic bidders to offset the
domestic duty /levies such as sales tax, octrois, etc. and certain disadvantages due to inadequate infrastructure and higher cost of
finance.  With zero customs duty from 6
th July 1999 for direct import by project authorities, the effect of price preference of 15% had
automatically been reduced to zero.
 
4.            Secretary, Ministry of Power, Secretary, Department of Revenue, Director General of Foreign Trade raised the following
objections:-
 
(i)  World Bank/ ADB had stopped funding power generation projects in India, the    rescinding of the aforesaid

73rd Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/73rdreport.htm[04-07-2016 12:15:38]
customs notification had no practical significance.
 
(ii)   If the domestic price preference is restored, the project cost will go up.
 
(iii)  If domestic price preference was restored, overseas bidders would not be interested   in competing for projects
funded by the World Bank/ADB.
 
5.            As regards point number 1 above, CMD, BHEL, drew attention to the press report appearing in the Financial
Express dt. 7.5.2002 where Minister of Power was reported to have stated that Government of India would seek financial
assistance of around $ 4 billion from ADB for implementation of various power projects.  If this was true, domestic
companies would be placed at a considerable disadvantage in the absence of domestic price preference.  Also, the power
transmission sector continued to avail of multilateral funding for its projects and domestic companies including BHEL were
already at a disadvantage while bidding for these projects.  In view of this, it would not be correct to conclude that the issue
had no practical significance.
 
6.            In so far as point number two was concerned, he stated that although the project cost may have the potential of
increasing to this extent, this may not happen in all cases, as this would depend upon the pricing strategies adopted by various
bidders in specific projects.  However, in the absence of domestic price preference and the consequent disadvantage suffered
by domestic industry, it was likely that more and more contracts would be won by the overseas bidders who would quote their
price in foreign currencies.  These companies would tend to adopt a different pricing strategy in the absence of effective
competition from capable domestic companies.  Also, as these projects got executed over a time frame of 3 to 4 years and
given the propensity of the Indian rupee to depreciate (past experience shows that, on the average, rupee depreciated @ 5 to 6
% p.a.), the completed cost of power projects was likely to go up by more than 3 to 4% on this account alone.  Also, if it was
considered that in all such cases, the spares and services for after-market maintenance of the equipment would have to be
imported, there was the likelihood of life time cost of the project going up by a factor much more than the perceived benefit to
domestic industry on account of domestic price preference.  Moreover, the overall economic cost involved in costly facilities
set up by domestic capital goods industry could not be ignored and the workers being rendered idle as a result of the domestic
price preference being denied to local industry.  India was one of the few developing countries (apart from China) to have
built up a capable capital equipment industry.
7.            Regarding point number 3, he stated that during the period from mid 70’s when multilateral funding of power
projects started upto July 1999, when domestic price preference was available to local industry in the case of projects funded
by the World Bank/ADB in the power sector, there have been 43 international competitive bids in all of which overseas
bidders competed.  Out of these, BHEL was able to win as many as 37 contracts registering a success rate of 86% without
availing itself of domestic price preference.  In any case, in the case of World Bank/ADB funded tenders, for evaluation, the
CIF cost of imported equipment was compared with the ex-works cost of domestic suppliers and the impact of customs duty
for imports as also excise duty for locally manufactured equipment were ignored.  In such a case, even if domestic price
preference were to be restored by withdrawal of zero customs duty regime, the overseas bidders should have no concern, as
the import duty attracted by their equipment would any way not be considered for evaluation of their bid.  As such, it was not
correct to say that restoration of domestic price preference by rescinding the aforesaid customs notification would affect the
overseas bidder’s interest in competing for World Bank funded power projects in India.
 
8.         The committee also heard Secretary, Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises, Dr. Adarsh Kishore, Additional
Secretary, Ministry of Finance (Department of Economic Affairs), Shri M.S. Krishnamoorthy, Head (Engg. Business), CII, Shri
Sarosh J. Ghandy, Chairman, IECIAL and MD (TELCO), Shri J.C. Mongia, Deputy Manager (ISGEC). 
 
9.            Chairman, IECIAL, also apprised the committee that the domestic companies were facing difficulties due to imports on zero
duty.  Representative of CII pleaded for more time to adjust to zero duty regime.

10.        After going into the details of the problems, the committee observed that a mechanism should be found so that
competitiveness of the domestic companies was not affected due to zero duty on imports.  The committee accordingly decided that a
Group of Secretaries under the chairmanship of Secretary, Department of Revenue, may be constituted to examine the issue of Duty
Free Goods and Services under the International Competitive Bidding with reference to Customs Notification No. 85/99 CUS dated

1          Agro and Rural Industries play an important role in the economy of our country. This sector  has vast potential in
terms of employment and dispersal of industries in rural areas. In view of its growing importance, the Ministry of Agro
& Rural Industries  was carved out of the erstwhile Ministry of Small Scale Industries and Agro & Rural Industries  
w.e.f. 1st September, 2001. The main function of the Ministry is to formulate policy measures for the growth of rural
industries for achieving rapid increase in gainful employment and balanced regional growth  which are among the main
objectives underlying the strategy of industrialization in the country. It also supervises and coordinates the activities of
different promotional agencies operating at the Central and State Level.
1.1       The various policies, programmes/schemes related to agro and rural industries are implemented through various 
organizations under the Ministry, namely, Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC), Coir Board and Small
Industries Development Organisation (SIDO) etc.
1.2      The Committee welcomes the formation of the new Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries. It has satisfied the 
long-felt need for the creation of   a new Ministry which would  look  exclusively  after the needs of this sector. This is
expected to  give a boost to the sector,  especially when our  industries  now face competition  from global companies 
and find it hard to survive.
1.3       Due to  the creation of the new Ministry of Agro & Rural Industries,  Demands for Grants for the Agro and
Rural Sector under  the new Ministry  have been dealt with  separately  in the budget for the year 2002-03. Earlier  , they
used to be the  part of the   budget allocation for the erstwhile Ministry of Small Scale Industries & Agro and Rural
Industries.

            KHADI AND VILLAGE INDUSTRIES  COMMISSION (KVIC)
 
3          The Khadi and village Industries Commission (KVIC)  is a statutory organization established in 1957 by an Act
of  Parliament. It plays a pivotal role in the strengthening of the rural economy by promoting and developing Khadi and
Village Industries. The objectives of the KVIC include skill improvement, employment generation in rural areas,
transfer of technology, rural industrialization and promoting self-reliance among the people, and to build up a strong
rural community base.
3.1       The functions of the KVIC are to plan, promote, organize and assist in implementation of the programmes for
the development of khadi and village industries. To achieve this, it undertakes :-
a)      Financing of eligible units and institutes.
b)      Training of  persons employed or desirous of  seeking employment in Khadi and Village industries and training
of personnel.
c)      Building  reserves of raw materials and implements, and supplying them at reasonable rates.
d)      Taking up R&D in Khadi and Village industry products.
e)      Encouraging cooperative efforts among   persons engaged in khadi and village industries
f)        The KVIC operates through 30 State/ UT KVI Boards, 5,599 registered institutions and 30,138 cooperatives,
188 departmental units and 15,441 sales outlets.
3.2       The Department related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry in its 49 th Report on Demands for
Grants (2001-02) pertaining to Ministry of Small Scale Industries and Agro & Rural Industries had expressed its
concern at  the inordinate delay in reconstituting  the Khadi and Village Industries Commission. The term of the
previous Khadi and Village Industries Commission expired in September, 1999 and since then the Commission had
been non-existent which adversely  affected the working of Khadi and Village Industries.  The Committee has been 
informed  that the Commission has been reconstituted w.e.f. 2
nd October, 2001.  The Committee welcomes the
reconstitution of the Commission and hopes that the new Commission will be able to take care of the requirements of 
the  Khadi sector to make it  self  sustaining and  vibrant.
3.3       The share of production generated under KVI programme, in the total traditional industrial activities of the
country like handloom, handicraft, sericulture etc., comes to around 7 percent. In the overall SSI sector,  the same is
about 1 percent.
3.4       The main objective of  creating KVIC was to generate employment in the rural areas through the artisans
working in cottage industries. KVI activities are providing a large number of employment to SC/STs and women. At
present,  32%and 46% of total KVI employment is from  SC/STs and women artisans,  respectively.
3.5      Keeping in view the importance of  rural industries sector for generating new opportunities of productive self-
employment the Hon’ble Finance Minister in his Budget speech to  2002-03  announced  that :-
“The promotion of rural industrialization would be helped greatly through capacity building and technology upgradation
in Khadi and Village Industries. To help in this effort, I propose to upgrade the Wardha Institute started by Mahatama
Gandhi in 1935 as a National Institute to be called Mahatama Gandhi Institute of  Rural Industrialisation.”
3.6       The Committee has been informed that  with a view to upgrade the Khadi and Village Industries Commission’s 
R&D Centre at Wardha i.e. Jamnalal Bajaj Centre Research Institute (JBCRI),  the KVIC has entered into a
Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT), Delhi with an investment of Rs.
8.35 crores, over a period of 3 years.
3.7       So far as the execution of work is concerned the IIT, Delhi has already started implementation of the DPR
(Detailed Project Report) as per the implementation schedule submitted to the Government.  Workshops on Quality
Assurance, Organic  and Herbal Foods, Rural Crafts and Pottery & Ceramics have been organized at different places.
Orientation Course for KVIC employees has also been conducted at the campus of JBCRI, Wardha.

74th Report of Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/74threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:15:39]
3.8       The process of deployment of manpower for the execution of work has also started and a Co-ordinator for the
project at Wardha has already been appointed.The institute is expected to have facilities for research, education,
extension and training.  The institute is also expected to prescribe quality standards for rural products and enable them
to stand in the global competitive marketing environment.
3.9      The Committee welcomes this move as it aught to provide a great fillip to  the sector. Simultaneously,  the
Committee notes that there is no specific provision in the Budget  for the required funds to implement  the 
announcement of upgrading the Wardha Institute  as a National Institute  named after Mahatama Gandhi. The
Committee is of the opinion that there is  a need  for additional provision of at least Rs.100 crores for the  Mahatma
Gandhi Institute of  Rural Industrialisation, Wardha. This provision may be  spread over a period of  three  years.
3.10    The Committee observes that R&D is the need of the hour if industries are to compete globally and growth in the
sector is to be stimulated. The Committee, therefore, recommends that allocation for Research and Development for
KVIC  requires  be increased.  If need be,  joint collaboration with foreign firms may be taken up.
3.11     Another important announcement of budget-2002-03 is regarding  Jai Prakash Rozgar Guarantee Yojana
(JPRGY). As a special concern for disadvantaged people in the most distressed districts of the country,  the Finance
Minister  announced that :-
“A Task Force headed by the Minister of Rural Development will be setup to design and implement a
massive programme for employment generation in these districts. KVIC, DC(SSI) and other agencies
will be fully involved in the implementation of this scheme.”
3.12    While appreciating this initiative,   the  Committee expresses its  concern that JPRGY should not meet the fate of
NPRI (National Programme for Rural Industrialisation) as announced in the Budget  for the financial year 1999-2000.
The allocation of Rs. 40 lakhs was kept for the NPRI  scheme in the B. E. 2001-02 which was reduced to nominal
amount of Rs. 1.00 lakh in the R. E. of that  year.  The scheme is yet to take off.  However, in the B. E. 2002-03 , a
provision of Rs 90 lakhs has been made. The Committee, therefore, impresses upon  the Ministry to review the progress
of  NPRI  so that the earlier  mistakes are not repeated by the administration.
3.13    The Committee is also unhappy to note that there is no concrete progress at all on the front of “Task Force on
Employment Opportunities” constituted in 1998. The Committee hopes that the Report of “Special Group on 50 million
new job opportunities” will be given due importance and properly implemented during the  Tenth Five Year Plan
period.
3.14     KVI Sector plays a very important role in the Indian economy. However, the recent lack of growth in  the Khadi
industry is a matter of serious concern,  especially in the light of declining production, sales, rural employment
opportunities and the share of Khadi in the total business of the KVIC. This assumes special significance as population
and per capita consumption of cloth in our country has increased over the years while per capita usage of Khadi has not
improved. One of the reasons for this could be that the khadi sector has not changed its products or even the product mix
in order to meet changing consumer expectations and preferences. It has, thus, not been able to exploit the full potential
of Khadi as a product category in all its forms.
3.15     The Committees feels   that for increasing sales of Khadi and providing greater and better rural employment
opportunities in this sector, it is necessary to provide and offer products that match consumer preferences.
3.16     The Government has recently taken the following new initiatives for promotion of this sector :-
-
                     “Khadi” is being registered as a brand name.
-                     The KVIC  is registering “Khadi” as a domain name also.
-                     The Government has advised the KVIC to register “Khadi” as a geographical indication.
-                     New products, new designs are being developed with the help of NID/NIFT etc. (National Institute of Design
and National Institute of Fashion Technology)
-                     Packaging of Khadi products is being improved.
-                     A mechanism to ensure quality of Khadi and V.I. products is being evolved.
-                     Offers have been invited to renovate the Khadi Bhawan in New Delhi to bring it at per with the any modern
international store.

74th Report of Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/74threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:15:39]
-                     Khadi shops are being planned at all international airports in India.
-                     Possibilities of marketing of KVI products through E-Commerce are being explored.
-                     Participation in national/international exhibitions.
3.17     As far as training is concerned, the KVIC conducts various training programmes for the entrepreneurs/artisans
engaged in KVI activities through its 48 departmental as well as non-departmental training centers. In order to improve
the quality of training and also to make it more meaningful to suit the changing requirements of KVI sector, the training
in KVI activities has been made a mandatory pre-requisite for any entrepreneur/institution desirous of implementing
KVI programmes.
3.18     In order to further strengthen the Khadi and Village Industries sector with a view to making it viable and vibrant
in the new era of globalisation, the Government announced ‘Khadi Package’ for the Khadi and Village Industries on
May 14, 2001.Details of the  package are as under:-
Option of Market Development Assistance and Rebate to Khadi  institutions.
Rebate policy for 5 years to bring in stability to the market as Khadi
institutions can plan their production and marketing.
 
 
            Term loan of Rs.300 crores under Consortium of Bank Credit (CBC)
Scheme to Khadi to be converted into working capital.
            Comprehensive insurance package has been worked out in consultation with
the insurance companies. It covers death, disease and disability .
            Steps have been taken to renovate a few major Bhavans of the KVIC.
            Standard logo introduced.
            A cell of the National Institute of Design has been set up in KVIC, Mumbai for
improved designs. Linkages have also been established with the National
Institute of Fashion Technology.
3.19     In collaboration with UNDP, projects amounting to 2.5 million dollars (around Rs 11 crore) have been launched
for bee-keeping, pottery, handmade paper and capacity building of KVIC.
3.20    The committee recommends that  KVIC should take immediate and concrete steps to take full advantage of  the
concessions offered    in the Khadi Package to it.
3.21     The Committee welcomes  the brand promotion by KVIC like `Khadi` and `Sarvodaya` The Committee observes
that  although  brand building  has traditionally been the   forte of  consumer products,  high technology companies too
have resorted to aggressive brand building especially the technology  sector like Microsoft, etc. Advances in 
technology, specifically,  the internet, will give further impetus to the creation of  global brands.
3.22     The Committee, therefore, recommends that KVIC should find out  (albeit through research)  the  products that
hold promise of creating value to the customers and should have  focused projection of these brands for better marketing
of KVI products.   The KVIC should propagate these  to reach out to the various customers  throughout the entire
country. The Committee hopes that brand name to various products under KVI sector will bring required  changes in the
marketing area of KVI products in the near  future. Further more,  to make their  produce acceptable, the KVIC should
improve and upgrade packaging particularly bottled products.   
3.23     For implementation of KVI  programmes, KVIC is  depending on the budgetary support provided by the
Government  of India and bank loans. The Committee has come to know that a line of credit of Rs.1000 Crore extended
to KVIC by a Consortium of Banks w.e.f. 1995-96 has  been stopped w.e.f. 8
th June, 2001. The reasons for this
stoppage is that  the bank loans were given in the form of a term loan,  but were used instead  as working capital by

74th Report of Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/74threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:15:39]
Khadi institutions resulting in an asset-liability mismatch. This forced  KVIC  to repay the bank loan without receiving 
payment from the borrowers.
3.24     The Committee, therefore, recommends that KVIC should  take steps to generate internal resources on its own so
as to reduce the dependence on budgetary resources of the Government as far as possible,  by evolving suitable
mechanisms like revamping of  KVIC staff, aggressive marketing of KVI products, brand building and other measures
so that it becomes self-sufficient and self-reliant. A long term strategy for suitable positioning of Khadi for the next 5-10
years needs to be prepared, otherwise the very survival of KVIC as an institution would be in doubt. 
 
3.25    As against a provision of Rs.106.30 crores in B.E. and R.E. 2001-02  for Khadi Industries, an allocation of 
Rs.70.65 crores in BE  2002-03 has been made.  Regarding reduction in allocation under Khadi grant from Rs. 106.30
crores in B.E. for 2001-02 to Rs. 70.65 crores in BE 2002-03, the Ministry has stated that funds of Rs.106.30 crores
allocated under Khadi Programme in the year 2001-02 under Major Head 2851 included a provision of Rs.105 crores
under Khadi grant,  and Rs.1.30 crores under S&T Khadi.  However, while reviewing the financial performance of
KVIC, it was observed that the Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC) had an unspent balance of Rs. 147.51
crores as on 31
st March, 2001. In view of the unspent balance of Rs.147.51 crores,  no funds could be released to KVIC
during the current financial year under Khadi Grant.  Keeping in view the trend of expenditure, the Ministry has kept a
budget provision of Rs. 70.65 crores only under this head for the year 2002-03 (a provision of Rs. 69.30 crore under
Khadi Grant & Rs. 1.35 crore under Khadi S&T).  In case there is improvement in expenditure, enhancement will be
requested at RE stage. 
3.26     Additional Secretary and Financial Advisor of the Ministry informed that “there were circumstances under
which the interest accrued  out of allocation for KVIC  was utilized for meeting  administrative expenditure. The present
sum has been because of the previous years, it has been built up over a period of time. This has not impacted on the
outlay for the current year, i.e., 2002-03. In fact, there has been an increase. This balance has been built up in the past
partly on account of the fact that adequate provision was not made for the administrative expenses of the KVIC. Hence,
there was a tendency on the part of the KVIC to hold back some part of the releases and use the interest earned out of
that for its administrative expenses. I would like to submit that we have now made structural rectification and now we
have  provided for the administrative expenses”.
3.27     The Committee views with concern that KVIC had   an unspent balance of Rs.147.51 crore   as on 31
st March,
2001. This is not a healthy trend as non-utilisation of money   earmarked for a specific  purpose does not   augur well for
the premier institution. The money should have been put to  better use.
3.28     The Committee recommends that in  cases where lapses had been continuing over the years,  responsibility
should be fixed and better budget management  undertaken. This would be a major step forward.   The Committee
recommends further that expenditure frame-work needs to be strengthened. This would involve identifying current and
future financial requirements, and deviations from the prescribed procedure should not be allowed under any
circumstances.  
3.29     Asked about increase in Non-plan allocation of Rs.50.57 crores to Rs.55.00 crores of KVIC, the Ministry has
stated that  KVIC has a total strength of  200 Officers and 2712  Non-gazetted staff spread all over India covering
Central Office, Mumbai, 36 State Offices/ Regional Offices and other Departmental Centres, like Training Centres,
S&T Centres, etc.  In addition, there are about 3154 pensioners under KVIC. The actual expenditure to meet the
committed expenditure of pay, allowances and pensions etc., has been Rs. 57.25 crores for the year 2001-02, out of
which Rs. 14.25 crores was for pensions. The estimated requirement for the next financial year 2002-03 towards
meeting the committed expenditure is Rs. 59.45 crores against which an allocation of Rs.55.00 crores has been made. 
Additional funds will be provided for at RE stage.
3.30     The   Committee finds that non-plan allocation for Khadi and Village Industries  shows an increasing trend. It is
also not managed efficiently  while KVIC is  over-staffed. The  Committee recommends that KVIC should undertake
trimming exercise for reducing surplus staff by extending VRS in order to curtail non-plan expenditure and to make the
institution economically viable.
3.31     The Committee has been informed that in view of the changes in  the new economic scenario, it was found
necessary to strengthen the KVIC structurally to enable it to face the challenges of globalisation. Under these

74th Report of Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/74threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:15:39]
circumstances, it was thought fit to conduct a study to restructure the entire KVIC  to make it vibrant and self-sustaining
without compromising its cherished objectives. As such a Study of the KVIC had been entrusted to M/s. Arthur
Andersen India Private Ltd. The report of the Study is under examination by KVIC.  In addition to these studies, an
evaluation study of Khadi programme has been conducted by the Tata Institute of Social Sciences (TISS), Mumbai who
have submitted their report very recently and the same is also under the examination of the  KVIC.
3.32     The Committee observes that the report of Arthur Andersen was submitted in September, 2000 and  is still under
examination by the KVIC. The Committee recommends that the examination of the report be expedited and a final view
be taken without further delay.
3.33     It appears from  the functioning of KVIC that it  is inefficient,  mismanaged  and over staffed. For example, even
in the last year, the inventory lying at various out-lets was to the tune of Rs.700 crores. The stocks have  piled up,
money is blocked and  sale has come to a stand still.  When asked to comment on this, Secretary M/o A&RI stated that 
that  KVIC  wanted  to dispose of this inventory by giving more and more discounts or through some other method to
generate cash. The Secretary further submitted that there are stocks worth of Rs.600 or Rs.700 crores and he had asked
the CEO of KVIC to give complete details as to  the original value of inventory, the amount of godown charges,
administrative charge, the cost of stock, since how long is it lying, etc. He assured that he would  intervene  and take the
matter  up with the people concerned and take steps to see that the dead stock is  cleared.
3.34     Regarding  the unsold stock, KVIC Chairman stated that inventory had come down by Rs.100 crores or so and
right now, it is Rs.650 crores., this was  spread over 7001 outlets; per outlet share came to Rs.10 lakhs. Stock
requirement for the outlets is Rs.350 crores worth goods, but KVIC had an excess stock of Rs.350 crores more. He was
taking steps with the package given. The Government had given  permission to sell this extra stock at heavy discount
and he would  go ahead with it.
3.35     The Committee expresses serious concern that the stocks of goods worth several hundred crores are lying locked
and unused.  Perhaps this is why, KVIC  has been experiencing working capital difficulties. If this state of affairs 
continues, KVIC  will not only be faced with resource crunch as the money remains locked up and stocks lying unsold
but also lose customer base as there will be no takers for the old stocks.
3.36     The Committee therefore  recommends that KVIC should dispose of the old stock as early as possible even by 
providing heavy discounts and recover money. KVIC may utilize the revenue earned on fresh inventory and recycle the
money. KVIC should keep fresh inventory as  old inventory  would not fetch much money.
3.37    The Committee observes that poor quality and poor designs have resulted in poor sales and accumulation of 
large inventories.The working cycle of production sales-cash-realization for Khadi is long and substantial funds are
blocked as working capital  for Khadi institutions. This has adversely affected performance.
3.38     The KVIC  set   up Central Cotton Purchase Committee (CCPC) for purchase of cotton. The CCPC in turn
constituted Regional Cotton Purchase Committees for actual procurement of cotton at the regional level.  The agreed
programme of the institutions approved by the Standing Finance Committee of KVIC, was the guiding factor in
deciding upon the quantity of the cotton to be procured in a particular year. Though the system was good it was perhaps,
the lack of periodical review by the CCPC that did not take care of the stock build up before approving the quantity to
be purchased in the following years.
3.39     In order to correct the distortion, the KVIC  has already taken corrective action by rationalizing the Cotton
Purchase Policy for year 1999-2000 and also issued the notices to defaulting institutions to pay the penal interest.

            COIR
5          Major activities undertaken by the Coir Board for the development of the Coir Industry are as follows :-
(a)
                Undertaking scientific, technological and economic research and development activities.
(b)               Collection of   statistics relating to exports and internal consumption of Coir and Coir products.
(c)                Development   of new  products and designs.
(d)               Publicity for promotion  of exports and internal sales.
(e)                Marketing of coir and coir products in India and abroad.
(f)                 Preventing unfair competition among producers and exporters.
(g)                Assisting in the setting up of units for the manufacture of products.
(h)                Promoting cooperative organizations among producers of husks, coir fibre, coir yarn and manufacturers
of coir products.
(i)                  Ensuring remunerative returns to producers and manufacturers.
 
5.1       India is the world’s largest producer of coir. The coir industry is labour intensive and provide employment to
more than five lakh persons of which women constitute 80 per cent. The production of coir and coir products has been
rising continuously. The production of coir fibre has risen from 2,96,000 metric tones in 1997-98 to 3,64,000 metric
tones in 1999-2000. The export of coir and coir products has also been increasing from Rs.238.93 crores in the year
1997-98 to Rs.313 crores in 2000-01. Though India is the largest producer of coir, its contribution in world trade is
small due to low technology. Only 30% of the coconut husk is utilized for coir production. Coir Board is taking a
number of steps to improve productivity, export potential and better utilization of the raw material. These are :-
·
  Significant Research and Development activities in areas like Coir Geotextiles for soil and water conservation
and Coirret for speeding up the retting process.
·  Blended fibres are used for more value added products and a wider product range. MoU signed with NID,
Ahmedabad for collaborative research on design and product development  which includes blending of coir with
other natural fibres like sisal, jute, palmirah, banana, pineapple etc.
·  Coir Board is providing increasing support for brown fibre activities. White fibre is restricted to Kerala only
while brown fibre is available in all the other coir producing states.
·  Coir board is promoting increased   mechanization for higher productivity.
·  UNDP project for technology   transfer, modernization and capacity building at a cost of US $ 846,000.
·  Export promotion    activities   like participation  in fairs and festivals are taken up by the Coir Board.
5.2       A new Market Development Assistance (MDA) scheme has been introduced in Coir Sector. This scheme has
replaced the existing "Rebate Scheme" and provides financial assistance @ 10 per cent to the Apex Cooperative

Societies, Primary Co-operative Societies, Public Sector Enterprises in the coir industry,  Showrooms/Sales Depot of
Coir Board on the basis of gross annual sales turnover.
5.3       Coir Industry was traditionally confined to Kerala due to the abundant availability of raw-material and natural
facilities for retting. It is a labour intensive, export oriented cottage industry employing 5.43  lakh people. The rapid
expansion of coconut cultivation in the non-traditional areas increased the availability of raw-material and consequently
the coir industry spread to non-traditional areas like Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and  Orissa and  West
Bengal.
5.4       In view of the growing competition in coir and coir products from the countries like Sri Lanka, China, Vietnam
etc. the coir yarn products have been removed from the purview of Minimum Export Price  (MEP)  from 17
th July, 
2001. This is the first step towards deregulation.
5.5       The five year EXIM policy announced on 1 st April, 2002 seeks to enable  Indian artisans, Cottage and Small
Industries to venture out overseas and adopt the world  as their market. The new  policy makes exports free, easy and
possibly rewarding. This  assumes special significance especially when India ranks low in global competition given
global slowdown and domestic recession. The Exim policy is comprehensive,  encompassing agro sector, cottage and
handicrafts and small scale sectors thus taking care of more than 80% the population living in rural areas.
5.6       The Committee, therefore, recommends that in view of the importance of this sector, diversified forms  of coir
products  and product-mix   should be attempted.  Research programmes should be undertaken by the Coir Board for
improving the quality of the coir fibre, for enhancing the export of coir products such as the green husk fibre produced
in the non-traditional coir producing areas using “coirret”. The Committee also notes that the market for  coir pith, a
waste material of the coir industry converted into one of the major export items in the list of coir products, remains 
untapped and the potential for the export of coir pith is excellent. The Committee, therefore, recommends that all out
efforts should be made to make  pith export achieve its fullest potential.
5.7       Nearly 80% of the coir workers in the fibre extraction and spinning sector are women. The production and
processing methods in coir  industry continue to be traditional. The coir industry has the potential to provide
employment at low investment cost and a large number of people from the socially and  economically weaker sections
of the society depend on this industry. It is for this reason that the establishment of coir industry in India gains added
significance.
5.8       During the BE 2002-03 Coir Industries have been allocated an amount of Rs.16.20 crores as plan and Rs.2.76
crores as non-plan (total 18.96 crore) against a plan provision of Rs.18 crores and non-plan provision of Rs.5.11 crores
in  BE 2001-02 and 11.60 crores as plan and Rs.2.62 crores as a non-plan in the RE for 2001-02.
5.9       The Committee observes that Coir Sector employs   5 lakh people and it has the potential of expanding its
activities. Although the fund allocation for the sector has been doubled in the 9
th five year plan from what it was in the
8th five year plan, (Rs.31 crores during the 8 th five year Plan and Rs.60 crores during the 9 th five year Plan), this sector
is still under-budgeted. There is further scope for absorbing funds in this sector particularly in the non-traditional areas
such as Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh, Orissa, West Bengal, Andaman and Nicobar Islands where new
products could be developed.  The Committee therefore recommends that the allocation for the Coir Industry should be
revised so that attention can be focused on providing more employment opportunities in this sector.   
5.10     For the first time in the history of coir industry, a Group Personal Accident Insurance Scheme has been
introduced in coir sector. Under this scheme a coir worker who meets with accidental death, permanent total disability
or partial total disability is eligible for compensation upto Rs. 25,000.
5.11     The Committee appreciates the measure for welfare of the people, especially women, engaged in the coir
industry which  remains unorganised to a great extent. The Committee hopes that more such initiatives  would be  taken
in near future  for the benefit of large number of people engaged in the industry.

TINY AND MICRO ENTERPRISES
9          Tiny enterprises are an important component of the SSI sector whose relative share in village and small
industries is increasing. The sector is important since it utilizes local raw material, provides employment to local
manpower and caters broadly to local market. This sector however, suffers from weak financial structure, use of
traditional and obsolete technology resulting into poor quality goods and having no access to the economies of scale.
These are basically one man shows and lack modern and efficient entrepreneurship.
9.1       The tiny sector enjoys distinct advantage of its ability to utilize local resource and skill. They cater to local needs
and generate substantial employment opportunities. However, they suffer from certain inherent weaknesses :-
(i)
                  Very poor capital base and difficulty in raising institutional credit
(ii)                Lack of infrastructure facilities particularly power
(iii)               Inadequate access to appropriate technology
(iv)              Problems in marketing the produce on account of quality, cost and inability to adopt    the required
marketing techniques
(v)                Inadequate competitive abilities
(vi)              Inability to cope up with plethora of laws, rules and regulations
(vii)      Lack of entrepreneurial skills and training
9.2       The Committee observes that tiny and micro enterprises are  the most  vulnerable sector in the era of free
imports and intense  competition.  The sector is most threatened  in the face of challenges thrown from China and cheap
imports from Nepal. Office of Development Commissioner (Small Scale Industries) should see that concern of tiny
sector are addressed  adequately and optimum assistance may be provided to them to tide over hurdles faced by them
like poor capital base, lack of infrastructure, obsolete technology marketing and competitiveness etc.  In view of the
importance of this sector, appropriate measures for promotion of tiny sector by the Govt. may be taken by reorienting its
policies.

            The Committee welcomes the formation of the new Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries. It has satisfied the 
long-felt need for the creation of   a new Ministry which would  look  exclusively  after the needs of this sector. This is
expected to  give a boost to the sector,  especially when our  industries  now face competition  from global companies 
and find it hard to survive.
      (Para 1.2)
 
            The Department related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry in its 49
th Report on Demands for
Grants (2001-02) pertaining to Ministry of Small Scale Industries and Agro & Rural Industries had expressed its
concern at  the inordinate delay in reconstituting  the Khadi and Village Industries Commission. The term of the
previous Khadi and Village Industries Commission expired in September, 1999 and since then the Commission had
been non-existent which adversely  affected the working of Khadi and Village Industries.  The Committee has been 
informed  that the Commission has been reconstituted w.e.f. 2
nd October, 2001.  The Committee welcomes the
reconstitution of the Commission and hopes that the new Commission will be able to take care of the requirements of 
the  Khadi sector to make it  self  sustaining and  vibrant.

(Para 3.9)
 
            The Committee observes that R&D is the need of the hour if industries are to compete globally and growth in the
sector is to be stimulated. The Committee, therefore, recommends that allocation for Research and Development for
KVIC  requires  be increased.  If need be,  joint collaboration with foreign firms may be taken up.
(Para 3.10)
            While appreciating this initiative,   the  Committee expresses its  concern that JPRGY should not meet the fate of
NPRI (National Programme for Rural Industrialisation) as announced in the Budget  for the financial year 1999-2000.
The allocation of Rs. 40 lakhs was kept for the NPRI  scheme in the B. E. 2001-02 which was reduced to nominal

Employment Opportunities” constituted in 1998. The Committee hopes that the Report of “Special Group on 50 million
new job opportunities” will be given due importance and properly implemented during the  Tenth Five Year Plan
period.
(Para 3.13)
 
            The Committees feels   that for increasing sales of Khadi and providing greater and better rural employment
opportunities in this sector, it is necessary to provide and offer products that match consumer preferences.
(Para 3.15)
           
            The committee recommends that  KVIC should take immediate and concrete steps to take full advantage of  the
concessions offered    in the Khadi Package to it.
(Para 3.20)
 
            The Committee welcomes  the brand promotion by KVIC like `Khadi` and `Sarvodaya` The Committee observes
that  although  brand building  has traditionally been the   forte of  consumer products,  high technology companies too
have resorted to aggressive brand building especially the technology  sector like Microsoft, etc. Advances in 
technology, specifically,  the internet, will give further impetus to the creation of  global brands.
(Para 3.21)
 
            The Committee, therefore, recommends that KVIC should find out  (albeit through research)  the  products that
hold promise of creating value to the customers and should have  focused projection of these brands for better marketing
of KVI products.   The KVIC should propagate these  to reach out to the various customers  throughout the entire
country. The Committee hopes that brand name to various products under KVI sector will bring required  changes in the
marketing area of KVI products in the near  future. Further more,  to make their  produce acceptable, the KVIC should
improve and upgrade packaging particularly bottled products.

(Para 3.22)
 
            The Committee, therefore, recommends that KVIC should  take steps to generate internal resources on its own so
as to reduce the dependence on budgetary resources of the Government as far as possible,  by evolving suitable

but also lose customer base as there will be no takers for the old stocks.

The Committee therefore  recommends that KVIC should dispose of the old stock as early as possible even by 
providing heavy discounts and recover money. KVIC may utilize the revenue earned on fresh inventory and recycle the

(Para 3.36)

            The Committee observes that poor quality and poor designs have resulted in poor sales and accumulation of

            The Committee recommends that the following policy support measures should be extended to Khadi and
Village Industries to give it  further boost :-
 
(i)               Most of the states have given sales tax exemption to KVI products,  however, Value added-tax is to
come into force w.e.f. 1.4.2003.  KVI Sector should be exempted from value added tax, octroi, entry tax etc.
 
(ii)     Existing labour laws, by and large exit to safeguard the interest of organized labour in large and medium
industries. High Power Committee headed by the thenPrime Minister Shri Narasimha Rao recommended
exemption of KVI sector from the existing labour laws as artisans are mostly self-employed. A policy decision 
in the matter should be taken at the earliest.
 
(iii)    Financial institutions have started playing important role from mid 1990s after introduction of REGP. But still
now the investment is very low compared to other areas in priority sector. Special earmarking for KVI sector is
felt necessary.
 
(iv)
      Preferential purchase support as is available to certain sectors is not there for KVI sector. The policy decision
for state and central governments to purchase a minimum percentage of utility articles from KVI sector will
give boost to the sector.
 
(v)
        Declaration of KVIC as Export Promotion Council for KVI products will promote export of KVI goods and
create potential for exports.
(Para 3.42)
           
The Committee observes that  in spite of KVIC’s repeated request over the years, funds flow to KVI Institutions
from Banks under ISEC is not upto the desired level. Analysis of ISECs  issued by KVIC  and actual funds made
available by Banks against the ISEC indicates that in the recent past the gap in the ISEC value vis-à-vis fund provided
by Banks goes to be extent of  50%.
(Para 4.2)
            The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Govt. of India/RBI may take appropriate policy decision so that
Banks are  bound to honour the ISECs issued by the KVIC to its full extent.
(Para 4.3)

            While addressing the concerns of KVI sector, the impact of globalisation, availability of latest technology,
multiplicity   and inadequate infrastructure have to be taken into account. At the same time, in order to meet the
challenges of   global competition, the Village Industries products have to be competitive in terms of quality, packaging,
pricing etc.  The Committee therefore recommends that continuous efforts need to be made for  improving the quality,
design and marketing of Village Industries products.  In order to achieve these objectives,   existing R&D facilities need
to be enhanced to facilitate Village Industries to introduce innovation, quality assurance and standardization. Last but
not least, a holistic approach is required  to be made to achieve the goal of  improving the functioning of KVIC.
(Para 4.4)
 
            The five year EXIM policy announced on 1
st April, 2002 seeks to enable  Indian artisans, Cottage and Small
Industries to venture out overseas and adopt the world  as their market. The new  policy makes exports free, easy and
possibly rewarding. This  assumes special significance especially when India ranks low in global competition given
global slowdown and domestic recession. The Exim policy is comprehensive,  encompassing agro sector, cottage and
handicrafts and small scale sectors thus taking care of more than 80% the population living in rural areas.
(Para 5.5)
 
            The Committee, therefore, recommends that in view of the importance of this sector, diversified forms  of coir
products  and product-mix   should be attempted.  Research programmes should be undertaken by the Coir Board for
improving the quality of the coir fibre, for enhancing the export of coir products such as the green husk fibre produced
in the non-traditional coir producing areas using “coirret”. The Committee also notes that the market for  coir pith, a
waste material of the coir industry converted into one of the major export items in the list of coir products, remains 
untapped and the potential for the export of coir pith is excellent. The Committee, therefore, recommends that all out
efforts should be made to make  pith export achieve its fullest potential.
(Para 5.6)
 
            The Committee observes that Coir Sector employs   5 lakh people and it has the potential of expanding its
activities. Although the fund allocation for the sector has been doubled in the 9
th five year plan from what it was in the
8th five year plan, (Rs.31 crores during the 8 th five year Plan and Rs.60 crores during the 9 th five year Plan), this sector
is still under-budgeted. There is further scope for absorbing funds in this sector particularly in the non-traditional areas
such as Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh, Orissa, West Bengal, Andaman and Nicobar Islands where new
products could be developed.  The Committee therefore recommends that the allocation for the Coir Industry should be
revised so that attention can be focused on providing more employment opportunities in this sector.   
(Para 5.9)
            The Committee appreciates the measure for welfare of the people, especially women, engaged in the coir
industry which  remains unorganised to a great extent. The Committee hopes that more such initiatives  would be  taken
in near future  for the benefit of large number of people engaged in the industry.
(Para 5.11)
 
            The Committee observes that only a third of the target  could be achieved in the case of PMRY during the year
2001-02 (upto December, 2001) It is inconceivable how the two third of the target could be achieved during the
remaining three months of the year. The Committee, therefore, recommends that setting of the targets should go along
with achieving of the same in a phased manner. If need be, efforts should be made for achieving of the target percentage
wise within a stipulated time frame.   
(Para 6.4)

            The Committee finds that target under PMRY set by the Ministry has remained static during the last four years
as shown above.  The Committee had hoped that with the creation of  new Ministry, the target and allocation for the
scheme would be increased,  but the Committee finds that the target set during the last four years of PMRY has remain
unchanged i.e   2.20 lakhs  The Committee therefore, recommends that taking into consideration the importance of the
scheme for employment generation,  target  for PMRY should be increased at the RE  stage and consequently the
allocation may be enhanced for the purpose.
(Para 6.7)
 
            The Committee observes that the crux of the problem lies in the recovery scenario under PMRY which has been
showing a  decreasing trend   If this sort of thing continues,  there will be less  funds available year by year  to
channelise for future schemes as the money will be in short supply. A stage  may come  that the  scheme may have to be
closed down due to non-availability of funds. The Committee, therefore, recommends   that recovery of loans,  which is
a grey area in the present scenario, should be given more attention and loopholes in this regard should be plugged  so
that the scheme may not be scuttled for want of funds in future  and recycling of funds may continue. The
Chairman/Managing Directors – All India Scheduled Commercial Banks may be suitably advised by the RBI to
improve their recovery performance to recycle the funds and constitute `recovery cells’ at Regional/ Zonal  office level.
(Para 6.9)
 
            The Committee further observes that though the Government achieved in some measure quantitative target of the
PMRY,  no efforts were made either by the Govt. or by other agencies to evaluate the qualitative achievement of the
scheme. The beneficiaries experienced difficulties in starting and running the venture. The major problem in starting the
unit was in getting the loan. 50% of the beneficiaries were affected by the delay in disbursement of the loan. This forced
them to take loan from  moneylenders  at a very high rate of interest and this had an adverse effect on their business.
The beneficiaries reported that because of the financial delay they could not reach  their  expectations. The beneficiaries
of the category made default in payment of loan.
(Para 6.10)
 
            The Committee finds that shortage of funds for working capital is hindering the PMRY beneficiaries. They could
not execute  their  orders in time due to shortage of funds and for marketing capital requirements, they resort to private
money lenders at a high rate of interest resulting in the increased cost of production and short fall in profit margin.
(Para 6.11)
 
            The high cost of operation is another problem where 20% of the industries were affected by this and  they could 
not compete in the local market. Increase in the cost of spare parts are the main cost accelerating items and
entrepreneurs could not  repay- the interest in time. The entrepreneurs could not adjust  themselves  to the demand and
supply mechanism of the market.
(Para 6.12)
 
            As regards the undue delay in giving loans by banks, the Committee impresses upon banks to avoid undue
delay.  The Committee recommends that implementing banks should be advised by the RBI to sanction the applications
within the prescribed time frame and speedily dispose off the same to ensure that there is no inordinate gap between the
sanction and disbursement of loan. DICs should play a pro-active role in this regard. RBI`s guidelines for disposing of
applications under PMRY within the time period of thirty days must be adhered to by banks.
(Para 6.13)
 
            As  regards the delay in getting power connection, the Committee desires that Government should take suitable

1.1       The Ministry of Small Scale Industries is the nodal ministry for policy formulation, promotion, development and
protection of small scale industries. It also monitors the implementation of these policies.
1.2       Ministry of SSI designs and implements the policies through its field organizations for promotion and growth of
small enterprises. The Ministry also coordinates with other Ministries/Departments on behalf of the Small Scale
Industries (SSI) sector.
1.3       Implementation of   policies and various programmes/schemes for providing infrastructure and support services
to small enterprises is undertaken through its attached office, namely the Small Industries Development Organisation
(SIDO).
1.4              Small Scale Sector is an integral part of the Indian economy. It has contributed significantly in the overall
economic development of the country and has provided vibrancy to its economy. Today, there are 3.2   million
registered small units in the country employing 18 million persons. In terms of value addition, it contributes 40 per cent
of the manufacturing sector production and its share in the total exports of the country is around 36 per cent. This sector
is the largest employment generator next to agriculture.
1.5              The overall performance of this sector during the last few years has been better than the performance of the
industrial sector as a whole. This sector has the potential to withstand change. It produces more than 8,000 items
varying from the simple to the most sophisticated products, using state-of-the-art technology. However, with
liberalization and opening up of the Indian economy, this sector is now facing tremendous challenges, albeit with
sufficient opportunities for growth.
1.6       The process of liberalization and market reforms has created wide-ranging opportunities for the development of
small-scale industries. At the same time, changing world scenario has thrown up new challenges to the very existence of
the sector. Moreover, this sector has also been facing some problems related to credit, infrastructure, technology,
marketing, delayed payments, problems on account of complex rules and regulation etc.  The need of the hour is to
suitably strengthen the sector so that it can adapt itself to the changed environment and face challenges boldly and
effectively. In order to enable this sector to avail the opportunities and play its role as an engine of growth, the Hon’ble
Prime Minister on 30
th August 2000 announced a Comprehensive Policy Package for the SSI Sector.
1.7       The small enterprise has emerged as a focus area for forging and promoting trade. Economic reform programmes
envisage the emergence of Indian Industry as a global competitor with substantial presence in the international markets.
Technology upgradation and modernization of SSI sector and promotion of export from this sector are interlinked
issues, which are important objectives behind promoting international cooperation. Nine countries viz; USA, Germany,
Italy, South Korea, U.K., Taiwan, Japan, Singapore and Israel have been identified as the thrust countries for promoting
enterprise-to-enterprise cooperation to upgrade the capabilities of Indian SSI sector to make it competitive in the global

VI.      CREDIT TO SSI SECTOR
6.1       One of the major problems of SSls is that of finance, whether it is equity, term loan or working capital. Financial
institutions and commercial banks are often reluctant to lend to small scale enterprises because of the high risks
involved. Moreover, the commercial banks and financial institutions that provide working capital and term finance to
the corporate borrower generally demand personal guarantees from borrowers, besides collateral. This adversely affects
the borrowing capacity of the small entrepreneur. The lack of coordination between commercial banks and financial
institutions causes delay in availability of working capital and hence in the commissioning of projects. The complex and
time-consuming procedures and formalities of the institutional lenders cause operational impediments for SSI units.
6.2       The Ministry has apprised the Committee that the net bank credit outstanding to SSI sector has increased from
Rs. 45, 789 crores as on 31.3.2000 to Rs. 48, 445 crores on 31.3.2001.  In order to further increase the flow of credit, the

a)      The limit for composite loans has been increased from Rs. 2 lakhs to Rs. 5 lakhs.
b)      391 specialised branches of public sector banks have been opened for small scale industries as of September 30,

c)      The exemption limit for collateral security has been increased from Rs. 25, 000 to Rs. 5 lakhs.
d)      The project cost limit under the National Equity Fund has been increased from Rs. 25 lakhs to Rs. 50 lakhs.
6.3       While welcoming these steps, the Committee feels that there is need for effective implementation of the
provision of these schemes by providing clear instructions. Banks had identified a time frame for clearance / rejection
(with reasons) of loan applications. However, they need to follow it sincerely. Further, once a loan has been sanctioned,
a time frame for the release of various installments should be committed in accordance with the needs of the
entrepreneurs. It must also be ensured that with the provision of the concept of single window, the time involved in
making the disbursements is considerably reduced. As far as the National Equity Fund (NEF) scheme is concerned, it
may be noted that the disbursements under the scheme are very small. The scheme needs to be made more effective and
efficient.
6.4       The Committee also recommends that SSIs branches of Banks should display prominently on the bank counters
that loans upto Rs.5 lakhs are available without collateral. This would dispel the wrong notion that loans are not given
without collateral.    
6.5       The Committee was apprised by the SSI Associations    that   too many holidays especially in the month of
March in Public Sector Banks, prove to be bottlenecks for the working of SSI units, which remain at the mercy of   the
Banks for their cash transaction.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that Banking Division, Ministry of Finance
should reschedule holidays of   Public Sector Banks in such a manner that public in general and SSI sector in particular
do not suffer   any more. 
6.6       Encouraged by the Kisan Credit Card Scheme, public sector banks have now decided to introduce a scheme
called Laghu Udyami Credit Card (LUCC) scheme for providing simplified and borrower friendly credit facilities to
small businessmen, retail traders, artisans and, small entrepreneurs, professionals and other self employed persons,
including those in the tiny sector.
6.7       The Committee hopes that this scheme is successful and that the small and tiny sector is able to derive
substantial advantage from it.
 
VII.     CREDIT GUARANTEE FUND SCHEME FOR SMALL INDUSTRIES
7.1       The Government introduced the Credit Guarantee Fund Scheme for Small Industries in May 2000 with the
objective of making credit available to SSI units, particularly tiny units, for loans up to Rs.10 lakh without
collateral/third party guarantees. The Scheme is being operated by the Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Small Industries
(CGTSI) set up jointly by the Government of India and SIDBI. The loan limit underthe Scheme, which was Rs.10 lakh
per borrower, has been enhanced to Rs.25 lakh per borrower in terms of the Comprehensive Policy Package on SSI
announced by the Hon’ble Prime Minister on 30
th August, 2000, when the Scheme was formally launched.
7.2       The Scheme covers collateral free credit facility (term loan and/or working capital) extended by eligible lending
institutions to new and existing SSI Units including Information Technology and Software Industry, up to Rs.25 lakh
per borrowing unit. The Guarantee cover would be up to 75% of the credit subject to maximum guarantee limit of
Rs.18.75 lakh. The lending institutions availing guarantee from theTrust have to pay a one time guarantee fee of 2.5% of
the Credit facility (comprising term loan and/or working capital) sanctioned by the lending institution to the borrower
and annual service fee of 1% per annum on the outstanding loan amount on 31
st March of each year.
7.3       The Credit Guarantee Scheme was initially approved for one year with a corpus of Rs.125 crore contributed by
the Government of India and SIDBI in the ratio of 4:1. Subsequently, the Government decided to continue the Scheme
beyond one year and increase the eligibility of loans to be guaranteed from Rs.10 lakh to Rs.25 lakh. Necessary
modifications have been carried out in the indenture of the Trust to enable Credit GuaranteeFund Trust for Small
Industries to guarantee loans up to Rs.25 lakh.  The Corpus fund of CGTSI was enhanced to Rs.200 crore with a further

7.5       The Committee observes that credit facility is one of the basic inputs that have to be provided to SSIs if they

VIII.     VENTURE CAPITAL FUND
8.1       The Committee observes that in order to encourage new entrepreneurs to set up small scale units, it is very
important to create Venture Capital facilities. With a view to meeting the needs of emerging areas and to help the small
scale units in Software / Information Technology sector, SIDBI has taken an initiative in the launching of the State /
Regional Level Venture Capital Fund with participation from State Governments. However, Venture Capital is not
easily available to very small and tiny units. EXIM Bank has also made an entry into venture capital finance by
investing in a Venture Capital Fund -India Technology Venture Unit Scheme -promoted by Unit Trust of India.
8.2       The Committee recommends that more venture funds in high-growth sectors such as information technology,
biotechnology and food processing should be set up. A suitable policy framework may be designed expeditiously to
promote setting up of such funds in the public as well as the private sector. Banks should be encouraged to entertain
Venture Capital funding to SSI units.   India can learn from the Korean experience, which has a very well developed
system of venture capital financing. The Korean Government has also made every effort to provide an atmosphere in
which a new concept company, the venture business, could take root during a short period of time. As a result, the
number of Venture Capital firms has increased tremendously in Korea during the last three to four years.

XI.       ANTI DUMPING MEASURES
11.1     There is expected to be large scale dumping of different products and flow of cheaper imports to Indian markets.
Imported consumer goods being of international standards in quality and competitive in prices are likely to change the
tastes of Indian consumers. It may prove to be a major factor in shrinking demand for local products. SSls are struggling
to restructure themselves, diversify production, adopt higher standards, and have collaborations for product designs or
brands or upgraded technology for their existence. There is ignorance among small scale entrepreneurs about
implications of WTO provisions in general and removal of QRs in particular. SSls did not get much time to adjust and
prepare themselves for increased competition and are thus in a precarious situation.
11.2     The Committee recommends that on account of almost all products coming under Open General License (OGL)
list, the Government may further strengthen the anti-dumping mechanism so that remedial measures may be initiated
expeditiously.  Countervailing duties and safeguard duties may be imposed in order to protect domestic producers from
cheap imports.  It may not be possible for SSIs units to function   in such a competitive market.  However, if they want
to grow from SSI level, all facilities available to them should continue for at least five years.
11.3.  The Representative of Laghu Udyog Bharati stated
“In the treaty with Nepal, I understand, we have put a clause that only those goods which are having some
manufacturing content   of Nepalese origin are exempt from our import duty. Actually what is happening is, so many
sham units are now being established there in Nepal and the goods are coming from Nepal and hurting the small-scale
