APPENDIX-I 
26 August 1993 
PRESS COMMUNIQUE 
The Trade Marks Bill, 1993 which was introduced in the Lok Sabha on the 19th April, 1993 
and published in the Gazette of India, Extraordinary Part II, Section 2, dated the 19th April , 
1993 has been referred to the Department Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Industry for examination and report. The Committee consists of 42 Members of both the Houses 
of Parliament is headed by Shri Moturu Hanumantha Rao, M.P. 
l11e Bill inter-alia propose to amend an consolidate a law relating to Trade Marks to provide 
for registration and better protection of Trade Marks for goods and services and for the 
prevention of the use of fraudulent marks. 
The Committee has decided to invite suggestions/comments from concerned individuals , 
organisations and bodies on the various clauses of the Bill. Interested parties are, accordingly, 
requested through this Press Communique to send their views in the form of memorandum for 
the consideration of the Committee latest by 15th September, 1993. Copies of the memorandum 
may be sent to Shri Tapas Das Gupta, Under Secretary, Department Related Parliamentary 
Standing Committee on Industry , Rajya Sabha Secretariat, Parliament House, New Delhi 
(preferably with 75 copies both in English and Hindi of the Memorandum). 
Copies of the Bill for reference purposes are available in Parliament Library , New Delhi and 
Libraries of all the State Legislatures in different States. Copies may 3lso be obtained on specific 
request from Committee Officer, Department Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Industry , Rajya Sabha Secretariat, Room No. 123A, Third Floor, Parliament House , New Delhi .

Recommendations/Observations in respect of which replies of the  Ministry of Mines   have not been received. (Chapter

NIL
(Chapter - I)
 
Recommendations/Observations, which have been accepted by the Ministry of Mines
 
 
Recommendation       (Para    2.3)
 
Objectives of JNARDDC
 
The Committee while appreciating the objectives for setting up the Research Centre for Aluminium Industries has
noticed during its visit that the Centre is well equipped with modern analytical facilities and process development
monitoring and control facilities in order to carry out research work in the areas of bauxite, alumina and aluminium
smelting. The Committee recommends that the Centre should strive its best to achieve its cherished goal and make all
efforts towards removing the problems being faced by the Indian aluminium industry. 
 
Action Taken
 
JNARDDC has  assured that it will continue to strive its best to achieve its cherished goals. In consultation with the
Indian aluminium industry it will continue all efforts towards solving the problems being faced and referred to it by the
industry. 
 
Recommendation          (Para   4.2)
 
On-going projects of  JNARDDC
 
The Committee notes the projects undertaken by JNARDDC and hopes that the efforts made by the Centre would be
utilized as the store house of all aluminium related “experiments and observations” and the knowledge and experience
derived of the efforts would be helpful in removing the problems of aluminium industry. The Committee also hope that
each project under study by JNARDDC must involve the highest degree of intellectual honesty as far as the relevance
and the purpose of the projects are concerned.
 
Action Taken
 
JNARDDC has always stood by the need for showing exemplary intellectual honesty in choosing and executing projects
for the aluminium industry. The Centre will continue to act in the most responsible manner and enforce the highest
standards of discipline and honesty in its dealings with the Indian aluminium industry. Protecting intellectual property
rights as well as ensuring the highest level of confidentiality of the results of the work done for individual customers are
the very pillars of the Centre’s functioning. These will be maintained at all costs.
 
Recommendation          (Para   5.2)
 
Thrust areas for R&D
 
The Committee understands the significance of adopting the practice of process monitoring and modeling to carry out
the research work in a result -oriented manner. The Committee, while noting the steps taken by JNARDDC regarding
the process development and product development, recommends that JNARDDC should carry on such research work
which may help aluminium industry in developing new designs of products with the help of product mix. The research

80th Report

work should lead to the evolution of process development for cost reduction. JNARDDC should make a survey of the
market demand and engage itself in such research work which might lead to development of products in accordance
with market demands. The new initiatives being envisaged may be taken up at the earliest.
 
Action Taken
An entire new Division with the name “Process and Product Development” has been created for this purpose. The
Centre is well aware of its responsibility to come up with new processes and products for the benefit of the aluminium
industry and will continue to strive to achieve this goal to the best of its ability. Towards this end, the Centre will be
bringing out several technology capsules for transfer to the Aluminium industry both big and small.
 
Recommendation    (Para : 5.4)
           
The Committee desires that JNARDDC should involve itself in such research work which would provide better quality,
speed up design engineering and lead to cost  effective production for the ultimate survival and growth of indigenous
Aluminium industry in the changing scenario caused by globalisation and liberalization. The globally emerging trends
that need to be implemented in aluminium industry may be addressed on a emergency basis in collaboration with
aluminium industry.
 
Action Taken
 
The Centre is in continuous touch not only with the major aluminium producers but also a number of small industries
particularly in the Vidarbha region (through the Vidarbha Industries Association) to promote the use of aluminium in
the country in the form of new products and better quality of existing ones. The Centre is very conscious of the need to
bring to India globally emerging trends in the aluminium industry, particularly newer technologies such as inert anode
and wettable cathode.  Almost the entire R & D work taken up by the centre for the Aluminium Industry is concerned
with improving the efficiency and speed of processes, quality of the product,   material and energy conservation,
minimizing environmental hazards reduction in overall cost of production and related issues.  It  thus addresses all the
concerns  expressed by the Committee. 
 
(Chapter - II)
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT DESIRE TO PURSUE
IN VIEW OF THE GOVERNMENT’S REPLIES:
 
Recommendation  (Para : 3.2 )
 
Projects completed by JNARDDC
 
The Committee notes the projects undertaken and its participation in various modernization and upgradation projects .
 
Action Taken
 
No action required.
 
Recommendation (Para 12.2)
 
Formation of core group of Indian aluminium industry
 
The Committee is of the view that regular interaction of scientists of the Centre with the experienced professionals from
IIT, EIL, TISL etc. to enhance the knowledge and experience of Scientists of JNARDDC in developing various models
for aluminium industries. If necessary, working core group involving the Centre’s Scientists and academic institute may
be formed. The Committee also recommends that scientists of various institutions may be invited to the conference and
seminars for the exchange of views on a regular basis.

Action Taken
 
The Centre has maintained continuous interaction with professionals of academic institutes, R&D organisations and
industry. Persons from the industry have earlier worked in the Centre for long periods on deputation. Persons from
academic and R&D institutes as well as industries are members of its Research Advisory Council, Project Monitoring
Cell, etc. which monitor the Centre’s research programmes. Person-to-person contact between the scientists of the
Centre and others from premier institutions in the country has been an ongoing process. The Centre has also been
inviting persons from the other organizations not only to participate in the conferences organized but also to deliver
lectures on relevant topics. These efforts will continue.
 
Recommendation (Para :15.2)
 
SWOT analysis of JNARDDC
 
The Committee acknowledges the unique position of JNARDDC oriented towards aluminium process metallurgy. The
Committee recommends that JNARDDC should take advantage of its opportunities and overcome its weaknesses by
expanding and diversify its activities and if necessary JNARDDC should induct trained experienced scientists from
various fields.
 
Action Taken
 
The Centre has been engaged in expanding and diversifying its activities
 
Recommendation          (Para  15.5 )
 
SWOT analysis of  JNARDDC
 
The Committee recommends that the Department of Mines should examine the issue of cheaper imports and get anti-
dumping duty imposed if dumping is found .
 
Action Taken
 
The landed cost of imported aluminium is more than the domestic price as on date.  So far instances of dumping have 
not come to the notice of Department of Mines.
 
 (Chapter - III).
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH THE COMMITTEE HAS NOT ACCEPTED
REPLIES OF THE MINISTRY OF MINES OR FURTHER RECOMMENDATION OF THE COMMITTEE IS
REQUIRED
 
Recommendation   (Para  : 6.4   )
 
Diversification programmes of JNARDDC
 
The Committee feels that JNARDDC should chalk out its diversification programme in such a way as to benefit the
aluminium industry in the short as well as long term. Since technology for setting of such plants is not available in India,
JNARDDC can play a vital role in developing such technologies. The Committee recommends that research may be
undertaken to develop and adapt new technology which may help setting up of small and medium capacity alumina and
aluminium plants.
 
Action Taken
 
This is a major thrust area that the Centre is keen on developing. It has already initiated steps to find the factors

responsible for the economic unviability of small capacity of alumina and aluminium plants.  Attempt will be made to
remove the bottlenecks that stand in the way of establishment of mini-aluminium plants in the country that would help
in improving the availability of aluminium in the country.
 
Further Recommendation
 
The Committee   is pleased to note that JNARDDC is keen on developing diversification programme in  such a way as
to benefit the aluminium industry in the   short as well as long  term.  JNARDDC has made its diversification
programme a major thrust  area and has also initiated  steps to find  factors responsible  for the economic viability of
small capacity of alumina and aluminium plants.  However, the Committee would like to know the  details   about the
steps taken to remove the bottlenecks that stand   in the  way of establishment of mini-aluminium plants  in the country.
 
Recommendation          (Para: 7.3  )
 
Seminar/Conferences
 
The Committee appreciates the efforts made by JNARDDC in conducting seminars and conferences and recommends
that JNARDDC should conduct such conferences and seminars more frequently. The Committee also recommends that
JNARDDC should make some nominal entry fee from all the participants in order to raise funds to meet its financial
requirements.
 
Action Taken
 
The Centre has already initiated steps for increasing the number of seminars and conferences that it proposes to hold
during the year 2002. The calendar of events planned includes short course / workshops and international conferences
practically every month of the year starting from April 2002. Adequate participation of industry in such courses is being
ensured and the registration fee collected is added to the fund generated by the Centre. The Centre gives the widest
possible publicity to these programmes by way of mailing circulars to over 250 industrial establishments, academic and
R&D institutes as well as through personal contacts and electronic means such as e-mail.
 
Recommendation (Para: 8.2  )
 
Training programmes and workshops
 
Conducting of training programmes and workshops provides a platform to scientists for productive interaction and
encourage them to gather knowledge and share experience. JNARDDC should charge a  nominal fee from the
participants for the training programme to generate revenue to meet JNARDDC’s non-plan financial requirements. The
Committee also recommends that JNARDDC should give wide publicity to its training programmes.
 
Action Taken
 
The Action Taken Notes  in respect of  Para 7.3  at  Sl. No. 7 may  please be seen        
 
Further Recommendation
 
The Committee  would like  to know the details of proposed  short  course/workshops and international  conferences  for
the  year 2002-03 and the likely outcome of  these workshop and conferences .  The Committee would  like  also to
know the amount of   fee collected as  registration amount upto  the date of such workshop and conference held.
 
Recommendation (Para : 9.3 )
 
Consultancy and testing services
 
The Committee while taking note of consultancy and testing services offered by JNARDDC, is of the opinion that

JNARDDC should generate sufficient fund to meet its requirement of non-plan expenditure by opening avenues for
generating revenue by providing consultancy services. JNARDDC may stress on service mix and service endowment by
giving due importance to diversification in consultancy services and exploring new ideas for generation of new projects.
The Centre should try to provide consultancy services outside the country as well.
 
Action Taken
 
The Centre has been making all out efforts to increase the testing and consultancy services that it provides to many
industries. To this end, a profile of the Centre has been published and a quarterly Newsletter is being brought out .  The
Centre is all set to provide such services outside the country as well. It has already provided such services indirectly to
one of the aluminium majors of the world during March 2002. Negotiations are on with another of the major aluminium
producers of the world to provide testing services.
 
Further Recommendation
 
The Committee is of the opinion that the Department of  Mines  should have informed the committee as to whom
JNARDDC has provided consultancy and testing  services  during  March, 2002 and the amount of  consultancy fee
collected `against the service  rendered.  The  Committee would also like  to know the details of negotiation  by
JNARDDC with other major aluminium producers domestic as well as  international.
 
Recommendation  (Para : 10.3   )
 
Service to Downstream Sector
 
The Committee is of the opinion that JNARDDC with its experience can provide quality service to the down stream
sector. Efforts for establishing the downstream processing laboratory (DSP) may be accelerated and the staff be
imparted necessary training and expertise.
 
Action Taken
 
With regard to establishing a Downstream Processing laboratory, the Centre has taken many concrete steps such as
ordering of equipment and recruiting specialist staff. It has also initiated steps to send its scientists and staff on training
programmes to acquire expertise in this area as advised by the Committee. Experts from other organizations have been
invited to the Centre for interaction with its Scientists.
 
Further Recommendation
 
The Committee  desires to know the  outcome of  `concrete  step' taken by JNARDDC for establishing the 
downstream   processing laboratory (DSP) for providing quality  service to the down stream sector.  The Committee
desires to know   also the progress made in regard to setting up of downstream process  laboratory   and details of
training imported  to  scientists and staff and their   expertise acquired  during the course of training.  The Department of
Mines  in its ATN to the  present Report would also  furnish the details of outcome of interaction between the  scientists
of the centre and the representatives  of other organisations.
 
Recommendation          (Para: 11.4)
 
Pollution control and environmental impact assessment
 
The Committee observes that the problem of pollution is one of the threats being faced by human society. JNARDDC
can make significant contribution for environmental impact assessment. Central Government may consider to entrust
with JNARDDC to undertake study on various forms of pollution and develop mechanism for pollution/waste
management and control. The Centre should be regularly in touch with other related Ministries.

                                                                                    REPORT
CEMENT INDUSTRY — AN INTRODUCTION
1.1       There was a wide gap between the demand and supply of cement during the Seventies. During that time the
major cement units were not motivated either to produce to their full capacity or to expand as cement production was
under both price and distribution control i.e., their entire production was under levy obligation on the rate fixed by the
government from time to time.
1.2       The then Central Government had been considering various measures for achieving rapid increase in the
production of cement by establishing a large number of mini cement units, as in the case of China, where it was found
that the working of mini cement units are highly successful.
1.3       In the existing situation, a perception grew that establishment of mini cement plants would usher in an era
resulting in exploitation of smaller limestone deposits, dispersal of cement production capacity all over the country,
reduction of burden on the railway, lower capital cost and quicker installation and higher employment especially in
rural, hilly and other inaccessible areas. The then Government accordingly constituted two working groups to make
suitable recommendations regarding the choice of technology, and provision for fiscal incentives to attract large number
of entrepreneurs to this field.
Criteria for Mini Cement Plants
2.1       The Government considered the reports of both the working groups and announced the following decisions in
their press release No. 9-98/78 Cem dated 4.1.1979 :-
                 1.  The capacity for the mini cement plant will be limited to 200 tonnes per day on 66000 tonnes per annum.
                 2.  The choice of technology to be utilised should be left to the entrepreneurs.
                 3.  In addition to the units which may be set up by the entrepreneurs in the private sector or by the State
Government in the joint sector, the Cement Corporation of India would also enter the field to set up mini
cement plants as a promotional effort.
                 4.  The ex-works price of cement produced by the mini cement plants would be the same as the price
admissible to new large sized plants, viz. Rs. 296 per tonne. This price was assured for a period of five
years from the date of going into commercial production.
                 5.  Mini cement plants will be allowed a rebate in the payment for a period of five years.
                 6.  While the mini cement plants will be subject to price control under the Cement Control Order, they will be
exempted from distribution control under the same order.
                 7.  Mini cement plants set up in hilly and remote areas will be eligible for additional excise duty relief and
cash subsidy on merit.
                 8.  Mini cement plants will also be eligible for all other existing incentives and facilities available under the
Income Tax Act or under other schemes offered by the State Government.
                 9.  Large houses and foreign majority companies will not be allowed to set up mini cement plants.

2.2       Taking a cue from the above Government notification and announcement made by the Central Government in
the 8th Five Year Plan about building of infrastructure in the country, 126 mini cement plants were set up in the State of
Uttar Pradesh to supply the much needed cement for the various projects. But due to variety of reasons, these units
became sick and unviable.
Study made by the Sub-Committee for the Ministry of Small Scale Industries

5.         Committee's findings, observations and recommendations
5.1       Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation made a study regarding mini cement plants financed by the Corporation. The
study report inter-alia  mentioned that the performance of the cement industry is closely linked with the industrial
growth of the country. In the period from 1993-94 to 1995-96, when the industrial growth was higher, the scenario in
the segment was bright. In 1995-96 with 11.7% industrial growth, the cement production grew at 10.6%. As the industry
slowed down in 1996-97, so did the cement segment. The same downward trend continued in 1998-99. According to the
industry sources, the current take-off position is inadequate to generate more profits, as the low price realisation is still
not matching the production cost. The recession in construction activity, low investment in major infrastructure projects,
rise in the cost of power cost etc. coupled with high borrowing cost has marked down the industry's earnings.
5.2       Another major constraint in this segment is excess capacity. During the growth phase of the industry, almost all
major players in this sector had gone for huge capacity addition. As a result, the installed capacity of cement industry
doubled in the last four years. In 1996-97 the installed capacity was 96.25 million tonnes, going up to 105.25 million
tonnes in 1997-98. Some additional capacity is still expected to be installed in the coming years. Due to the huge
capacity available with major plants, they have encroached upon the segment of the mini cement plants by entering the
remotest areas. Mini cement plants, which traditionally used to cater to the local markets of remote areas, were
therefore, badly affected.
5.3       The study report further mentioned that the immediate future is not very encouraging. However, once the
Government starts the revival of the economy through investment in infrastructure and construction activity picks up,
the demand for cement will grow.
5.4       The Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation also entrusted ICRA with the job of preparing a report on the cement
sector. The ICRA had cited high interest rate charged by Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation as one of the problems
faced by the SSI units in cement sectors.
5.5       The Committee observes that the State Government had revised the rate of interest from 13.5% to 19.75% in
1991-92. The reasons for charging high rate of interest by Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation was due to the fact that it
got loans from SIDBI/IDBI at a higher rate. The Committee, however, feels that revising the rate of interest was not in
the interest of mini cement plants. The Government should have calculated the viability of those projects before revising
the rate of interest as it proved a disincentive for SSIs in the cement sector. As regards giving loans by SIDBI/IDBI on
higher rate of interest to Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation, the Committee observes that the U.P. Administration with
SIDBI/IDBI should have sorted out the matter.
5.6       The Committee notes that SSIs engaged in this business took loans from the financial institutions/banks, but due
to industrial slow down and stiff competition from giant plants they have to dispose of their products through distress
sale, which contributed to accumulation of interest against the principal amount of loan. Rising of interest by
Government under such circumstances proved to be the death knell for the SSIs in the cement sector. The Committee
further notes that Rajasthan Financial Corporation, under a one-time settlement, not only waived the interest completely
but also waived 20% principal amount so that the mini cement units situated in Rajasthan may survive.
5.7       In comparison, the units of Uttar Pradesh are working in a climate of apathy. Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation,
in a letter dated 4.10.2000 addressed to "Udyog Bandhu" (A Forum of Industrial Associations), mentioned that the
members of the mini cement plants association desired that whatever repayment (by way of interest or repayment) they
have made till date to the corporation may be adjusted towards principal and balance may be recovered from them in
easy instalments. The Board had already rejected this proposal earlier. However, if there is any demand of the
association for waiver of total or part of interest, the same is to be taken to the Board again for its approval.
5.8       The Committee fails to understand as to why Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation is not able to bail out the units
in UP taking a cue from the RFC when the units in UP are struggling for survival.

5.9       From the memorandum submitted by the Association, the Committee notes that problems of the units were to be
deliberated by a High Power Committee under the chairmanship of the Chief Minister. In this regard, the Directorate of
Industries, UP, in their letter dated 1.8.2000 requested Secretary, UP Administration, to place the matter before the said
High Power Committee. It appears that such a sensitive matter was not brought before that Committee. It reflects lack of
coordination between the departments of the Government. Similar situations also prevail at the central level also. On
various occasions, the Committee observed that various ministries did not have on integrated approach to solve the
problems of the industry. The Committee observes that if SSI units are to be given a boost, the different departments of
the State Government and Central Government are to work in a coordinated manner.
5.10     Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation portfolio has, at present, 48 cement-manufacturing units. Out of 48 units only
2 units are regular in payment whereas 1 unit has recently gone in production. As per the study conducted by the Uttar
Pradesh Finance Corporation, these units are facing problems relating to market recession like in transportation cost,
wage cost ban on mining, unimplemented units, temporary default, etc. The Committee notes the plethora of problems
being faced by the cement units. In the circumstances, the Committee observes that the reported harassment of these
units, instead of reviving them by the Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation, as mentioned by the Association, needs to be
looked into.
5.11     The Central Government had announced in the 8th Five Year Plan about construction of double express
highway, houses for millions, generation of power to take the electricity to the rural areas. Had such activities relating to
infrastructure building arisen, the present state of low intake of Cement would not have arisen. In fact, market demand
of cement was not in line with the Government's projection. In subsequent budgets of the Central Government the above
schemes did not find place, resulting in decline of demand of Cement.
5.12     The giant units which take 5-6 years to produce cement started production on in 1996 in UP after taking
financial assistance from IDBI on easy terms and flooded the market with cement at a cheaper rate and ousted smaller
units by waging an unfair and unequal competition. Had the development work regarding building up infrastructure
started before 1992 or during 1992-96 the smaller units would have survived and established themselves.
5.13     The Central Government had facilitated in establishing the mini cement plants to meet the demand of cement in
the emerging scenario of building up of infrastructure facilities in the country by enabling the SSI sector to get loans
from the IDBI. In all, 126 units were set up, of which 50% were in the category of integrated units (which produced
cement out of its own manufactured clinkers) and 50% were in the category of grinding units (which ground clinkers to
produce cement after purchasing clinkers from the big units). This method of producing cement by the SSI sector
received a setback when the Supreme Court banned mining of limestone and as a consequence, limestone mines were
closed in Dehradun. As a result, the supply of major raw material i.e. limestone, had stopped and self-producing
capacity of units for making clinker vanished. The remaining units are doing only grinding by purchasing clinker from
the big units. The woes of SSI sector did not end here. The capacity to produce clinker and producing cement out of
clinker has not only been taken away by the big units from the SSI sector, the price of clinker sold by them to small
units has been raised to such an extent that either the small units are unable to purchase it from big units or if they
purchase and grind them, they would not be able to sell that cement in the market because of high cost of production,
resulting in closure of mini cement plants.
5.14     Recently, the UP Government had offered 100% concession of Sales Tax for 12 years to those industries whose
investment is over PSUs crore. Under this scheme, the giant cement industries like ACC and Satna Cement have
established their grinding unit of total 8.6 lakh tonnes per annum capacity in Rai Bareily District of UP and are availing
of this concession. The State Government would lose a huge amount of revenue by granting this concession to the giant
units. The cement so produced after grinding by the giant units is much cheaper and their selling price is much lower
than that of mini plants. All the more, the giant units are availing double concessions: -
                (a)  Firstly, as a manufacturer of intermediate product i.e. clinker, they are availing sales tax exemption in
their parent state; and
                (b)  they are availing sales tax concession in UP as a manufacturer of cement.
5.15     During the course of oral evidence before the Sub-Committee, the SSI association expressed the apprehension

that those giant industries would leave UP after 12 years and establish their units in other states to avail sales tax
concession. The Committee was informed that small units are given only two years sales tax free concession as against
12 years to the giant units.
5.16     Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation's letter dated 4th October, 2000 addressed to "Udyog Bandhu" corroborates
the above fact. The study made by ICRA had concluded that integrated mini cement units were not viable. The report
further concluded that in case the unit took up grinding function alone, the operation could become viable with some
incentives. The study had further concluded that the units could be marginally viable if they were granted total sales tax
exemption. It has been further mentioned that Government of UP had granted 12 years sales tax exemption to big units.
The revenue loss to Government from these two units along would be Rs. 345 crores. It had been reported that there was
a third new large unit coming up in the State. Revenue loss from this unit alone would be Rs. 691 crores.
5.17     The above communication is the testimony of the fact how small units are discriminated against and have been
forced to wage a battle against stronger competitors.
            When the small units were gasping for oxygen, UP government issued a circular in 1998 asking its cement
consuming departments to send their demands to small-scale industries only. In spite of this, Government departments
are not complying with the order. As a result, the order remained on paper only without any visible results. The
Committee feels that a mechanism to monitor the compliance of the Purchase Preference Policy should have been
evolved if the Government really wanted to help the SSI sector. The Committee observes that an early action to monitor
the compliance of the order even now may save the situation for the dying SSI units.
5.18     Another factor, which has crippled the mini cement plants, is the lack of credit flow to the sector. While the giant
units had no difficulty in securing loans from banks and FIs, the small units are still struggling to get loans from banks
even after the announcement made to the effect that loan would be given without any collateral security. In addition,
restriction on load carrying capacity of trucks proved to be a strangulatory provision for the mini cement plants.
6.1       In nutshell, a vision was created during the successive Five Year Plans and notifications issued in 1979 that huge
infrastructure would be created nationwide but large cement plants would not be in a position to supply the required
quantum of cement. SSI sector was encouraged to set up mini cement plants to meet the demand of additional quantum
of cement in view of its lower capital cost, quicker installation and higher employment potential coupled with the
exploitation of smaller limestone deposits by it in rural and hilly areas. The banks gave these units loan assistance and
FIs and they started setting up units when the cement industry was hailed as the harbinger of overall development of the
state. The good days for the SSI sector did not last long due to economic recession when construction activities come to
low ebb.
6.2       SSI's cup of sorrow was full when the Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation increased the rate of interest from
13.5% to 19.75% and the giant units flooded the market with their brand of cement at a much lower price than that of
mini cement plants which in turn were forced them to sell cement at a price lower than their cost of production. They
failed to pay interest on the principal amount and the banks and FIs shut their doors to these sick units.
6.3       Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation made a study about problems and possible revival scheme of mini cement
plants through ICRA, which suggested complete waiver of interest coupled with full exemption of sales tax and
imposition of 15% price preference for the revival of mini cement plants. But so far, no positive step has been taken to
save the industry.
6.4       The Committee observes that in the recent past, there has been an overall increase in the rate of growth in the
cement industry. This is an indication that construction activity has again picked up. But these activities are confined to
certain places in the country and, by and large, large industries are able to reap the benefit of such a situation. The
renewed demand for cement has not percolated to the lower level of the industry. The Committee feels a lending hand
should be given to those sick units. Ways and means should be explored to bail out them from then pathetic situation.
6.5       The Committee also notes that as per norms specified by the Reserve Bank of India, a sick unit is considered as
potentially viable, if it would be in a position, after implementing a relief package spread over a period not exceeding
five years from the commencement of the package from banks, financial institutions, Government (Central/State) and
other concerned agencies, as may be necessary, to continue to service its repayment obligations as agreed upon
including those forming part of the package, without the help of the concessions after the aforesaid period. The

6.6       In view of the RBI guidelines, the Committee recommends that Ministry of Small Scale Industries, in
consultation with the RBI, Lead Bank Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation, and UP Administration should make an
attempt to revive these units keeping in view the ICRA report as well as action initiated by the Rajasthan Financial

REPORT
 
I.          Introduction
 
1.1       The Department Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry in 2002, appointed the following Sub-
Committees for detailed examination of Annual Reports:
            (i)         Sub-Committee I
            (ii)        Sub-Committee II
Sub-Committee III
Sub-Committee IV
                       
1.2       The Sub-Committee on Heavy Industry and Public Enterprises, as part of examination of the Annual Report of
Ministry of Heavy Industry and Public Enterprises, took up the examination of MoU system.
 
1.3       The Sub-committee, for a detailed study of the   MoU system and its effectiveness with regard to the
performance of the PSEs took up PSEs, of various Strategic sectors. 
 
BEML, Bangalore 
HAL, Bangalore
NPCIL,  Mumbai
 
As a part of examination of MoUs of PSEs of strategic sector, the Sub-Committee visited Bangalore to have first hand
information on the implementation of MoUs in BEML and HAL from 10
th – 11th June 2002.  The Committee also
visited NPCIL on 3rd July 2002 at Mumbai.   Extensive discussions were held with the Chief Executives of selected
PSEs and the Officials concerned with the MoU system. 
 
II.         BACKGROUND OF MOU SYSTEM
 
2.1       The Department of Public Enterprises in their Background Note on the MoU system have stated that as a major
policy initiative, the MoU system was introduced by the Central Government as an important tool to improve the
performance of the Central Public Sector Enterprises (PSEs).  The New Industrial Policy of 1991 laid greater emphasis
on the MoU system requiring all PSEs to be brought under the ambit of the MoU system.  Beginning with 4 PSEs in
1987-88, the MoU system has now been extended to a large number of PSEs during the course of time and during the
year 2000-2001, 108 PSEs have signed the MoUs.
 
2.2       It was stated that the main objectives of the MoU system are to improve the performance of the PSEs by
imparting increased autonomy and accountability and to provide a method of evaluation of the performance of the
managements of the PSEs in an objective and transparent manner.  Further, the objective of providing clarity of goals to

82nd Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/82ndreport.htm[04-07-2016 12:16:44]
be achieved by PSEs is another dimension of the MoU system.
 
2.3       The Committee has noted that there is a High Power Committee (HPC) at the apex level, headed by the Cabinet
Secretary which is basically a policy making body for the MoUs.  This HPC consists of Secretaries of all nodal
Departments of Government such as Finance, Expenditure, Planning Commission and Programme Implementation, etc. 
The HPC undertakes the evaluation of the performance of the PSEs and in addition the HPC also provides a forum to
resolve inter-ministerial issues.
 
2.4       To assist HPC in this task and also to provide the technical inputs and to finalise the MoUs, there is an Advisory
Body called Adhoc Task Force (ATF), it was stated.  The members of the ATF are drawn from various fields having
vast experience in their areas and include retired Secretaries, Chief Secretaries, top experts in different disciplines like
finance, management, science and technology, and prominent academicians.  This body provides the neutrality and
objectivity to the MoU system.
 
2.5       The Department have also informed that under the present set up there is a small MoU Division under the
Department of Public Enterprises, Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises, which co-ordinates the entire
exercise of finalizing the MoUs in respect of all the PSEs numbering 108. In addition to finalizing the MoUs, the MoU
Division is also responsible for the evaluation of performance of PSEs, both on the basis of the provisional results as
well as the audited results.
 
2.6       Explaining about the process of preparing MoUs, the Department have stated that the MoU process starts with
the issuing of guidelines by the DPE to the PSEs/Administrative Ministries for drafting the MoUs.  The PSEs prepare
their MoUs on the basis of these guidelines and these draft MoUs are then discussed with the Administrative Ministries
and in the Boards of the PSEs and are then submitted to the DPE.  DPE prepares background papers and its comments
on each draft MoU keeping in view the past performance of the PSE, its future potential, the industry scenario and the
economic environment of the PSE, it was added.  It was further stated that these draft MoUs are discussed in the MoU
negotiation meetings where the ATF members, managements of the PSE, officials from the Administrative Ministries
and the representatives from nodal Government Agencies like Ministry of Finance, Ministry of Statistics and
Programme Implementation and Planning Commission are also present.  The MoUs and the targets are finalised in these
meetings through mutual discussions.
           
III.       PERFORMANCE OF MOU SYSTEM IN THE STRATEGIC SECTOR
 
            The Sub-Committee now deals with the performance of MoU system of BEML HAL and  NPCIL in the
succeeding pages.
 
IV.       BHARAT EARTH MOVERS LIMITED, BANGALORE
 
4.1       Bharat Earth Movers Limited (BEML) came into being in May 1964 as a Public Sector Undertaking, with the
transfer of its present Bangalore Complex (formerly known as Rail Coach Division) from the Hindustan Aircraft
Limited, Bangalore. BEML is a company under the administrative control of the Department of Defence Production &
Supplies, Ministry of Defence. The Registered Office of the Company, including Marketing Headquarters, is located at
Bangalore. BEML commenced its operations from January, 1965 with the production of rail coaches and assembly of
spare parts at the Bangalore complex.
 
4.2       Since March, 1992, the company status has changed to a “Partly Owned Government Company” from “Wholly
Owned Government Company”. Presently, the  Government owns 61.2 percent of the total equity.
 
4.3       BEML is managed by a Board comprising Directors and headed by a Chairman and  Managing Director.
 
4.4       PRODUCTION UNITS
 
            The company has manufacturing units established at Kolar Gold Fields (KGF) Mysore and Bangalore – all in the
State of Karnataka.

4.5       KGF COMPLEX
 
KGF Complex comprises three manufacturing units, viz., Equipment Division, Heavy Equipment Shop and Hydraulics
and Power line Division. The Equipment Division has been producing since 1968 wide range of earthmoving equipment
such as Mounted Bulldozers, Hydraulic Excavators, Wheel Dozers and Loaders, Pipe Layers, Tyre Handlers and
Hydraulic Cranes. A recent addition has been Engineering Mine Ploughs. The Heavy Equipment Shop, with
sophisticated facilities, manufactures heavy earthmoving equipment like giant Walking Dragline, Electric Rope Shovel,
Higher Capacity Excavators, Dozers and other major welded structures. The Hydraulics and Power line Division, set up
in 1986-87, manufactures Transmissions and Allied Assemblies.
 
4.6       MYSORE COMPLEX
 
Truck Division produces different capacities of earthmoving equipment such as off the highway Rear Dump Trucks,
Motor Graders and Water Sprinklers. Aircraft Towing Tractors and Aircraft Weapon Loading Trolley. The Engine
Division manufactures different capacities of diesel Engines required for earthmoving equipment produced by BEML.
 
4.7       BANGALORE COMPLEX
 
            The Bangalore complex production unit manufactures various types of railway products such as Rail coaches,
Tower Wagons, Treasury vans, Rail bus and Milrail Coaches and Wagons for Indian Railways and the Ministry of
Defence. It also manufactures defence vehicles and aggregates such as BEML-Tatra Heavy Duty Truck/its variants for
tank transportation, ground support vehicles for integrated guided missile development projects viz., Prithvi, Trishul,
etc., vehicles for radar mounting, Field Artillery Tractor and Crash Fire Tender, Pontoon Bridges, Tank Transportation
Trailers and Ejector & Air cleaner assemblies BEML has been nominated as the Nodal Agency for Tatra family of
vehicles and also 155mm self propelled (tracked) gun system  (BHIM T-6).   BEML   reached a level of 49 percent  of
its total sales for defence sector in 2001-02. The Details are as follows:

4.8       FINANCIAL PERFORMANCE AND ORDER BOOK STATUS
 
The turnover of the Company started with Rs. 5.17 crores in 1965-66 and crossed the Rs.1421 crore mark by end of
March, 2002. Since its inception, the company has been making profits. The financial performance of the company for

from its inception. The year 2000-2001 was one of mixed fortunes. Subdued market conditions, worldwide recession,
liquidity crunch, and increased competition. US sanctions and a  host of other negative factors brought in considerable
strain on  business. Likewise, liberalized imports of capital goods, anomalies in custom duty tariffs adversely affected
the industry. Despite all these odds BEML share of EM (Earth Mover) business in 65percent out of total sales turnover.
Defence share in the sales turnover has gone up considerably to 49 percent.
 
4.9       QUALITY

            All the manufacturing divisions of BEML and its subsidiary units have been accredited with ISO 9001
certifications.
 
4.10     RESEARCH & DEVELOPMENT DIVISION
 
            The Company has a strong base of in-house design and development. The company’s R&D division at KGF has
successfully designed, developed and produced a range of new products.  The R&D division is making continuous
efforts to assimilate and update  technology. The activities of R&D include import substitution, cost reduction and
product development for the domestic and export market. Products developed by R&D have been exported to the UK,
Syria and West Asia.
 
4.11     MARKETING
            The Registered Office of the company, including Marketing Headquarters, is located at Bangalore.
 
4.12     EXPORTS
            BEML’s products are exported to West Asia, Syria, Tunisia, UK, South Africa and Jordan. A total of Rs.116.65
crores worth of products were exported during 2001-02, including deemed exports.
 
4.13     PERSPECTIVE PLAN
            The Ministry has approved the perspective Plan of BEML. A growth rate of around 8 percent per year has been
envisaged in the plan keeping in view the prevailing market conditions and areas of diversification possible in the
coming years. New products envisaged in the perspective plan include port equipments, material handling equipments,
road construction and mining equipments, mine ploughs, BHIM T-6 with 155mm gun, etc.
 
4.14     MOU of BEML
            The Memorandum of Understanding between Bharat Earth Movers Limited and the Department of Defence
Production and Supplies, Ministry of Defence, is an agreed document setting out the mission and objectives along with
performance parameters for monitoring and evaluating the performance of Bharat Earth Movers Limited for 2001-2002.
It also indicates assumptions and assistance expected from the Government in achieving MoU performance level.
 
4.15     MISSION:
            To be a leader in the field of development, manufacturing and marketing of state-of-the-art heavy engineering
products and also make presence in global market through quality, reliability, customer orientation with thrust on
profitability.
4.16     OBJECTIVES:
To maintain BEML’s role in the supply of engineering goods and services to the core sectors of the Indian economy.
To retain 60 percent market share of Earth Moving and heavy-duty vehicles in domestic markets with a well-knit
dealership network region-wise with a view to ensure after-sales service and product support for attaining utmost
customer satisfaction.
To improve profitability with a view to get a fair return on Capital Employed by year 2002-03.
To maximize physical exports with a gradual growth of 10 percent - 20 percent and develop regional export markets.
To achieve minimum 25% contribution to the  Defence Sector.
To reduce cost through improved efficiency and productivity.
To improve the quality of products and after-sales service.
To continuously review and implement up-gradation of technologies in respect of product-lines, facilities and
diversification plans to cater to the needs and demands of the market.
To concentrate on diversification of product-mix in Bangalore Complex with a view to optimize utilization of plant and
machinery and manpower for improving the profitability of Bangalore Complex at optimum level.
To reduce the Cost of Capital and Capital Employed.
To concentrate on infrastructural development through thrust on Road Building Equipments.
4.16.1  In the MOU, in addition to the profit related financial parameters, dynamic criteria such as Inventory Control,
Customer Satisfaction, Sundry Debtors, Delivery Schedule Adherence, Technology Development and R&D have also
been included. In addition, new criteria such as Indigenisation, IT initiatives, Patenting and benchmarking have also

been incorporated in the MOU to improve the performance of the company.
 
The details of targets and achievements under major parameters in respect of BEML are at Annexure-II and the MoU
ratings of BEML are given at Annexure-III.
4.17                 DISCUSSIONS WITH THE MANAGEMENT OF BEML
 
4.17.1  The convener Dr. B.B.Ramaiah, appreciated the performance of BEML in context of the company having made
profits since its inception.He,however, expressed concern over the fact that the rate of profit have been declining over
the years and the very survival of BEML is going to be at stake if this trend continues. Dr. K. Aprameyan, the CMD,
apprised the committee of the work being done by BEML mainly on BEML’s strength in multirole vehicles, transport
trailors which have found total acceptance with the defence forces. He further informed that BEML has carved a niche
for itself for its rugged products and at the moment, it commands a major share in the domestic earthmover industry.
The Committee was apprised that BEML has a vast range of heavy duty trucks with great amount of operational
flexibility and functional adaptability. Besides, BEML has vehicles, which are used for tank transportation including
vehicles which can move payload upto 10,000 kg weight. BEML also has a marked presence in all terrain vehicles,
which involve mounting of radar and bridge laying systems. BEML has equipments which can be used in case of
emergencies like earthquakes and BEML has done significant work during the Gujarat catastrophe.  The Committee was
informed that BEML has developed vehicles that can be fitted with multifunctional cranes and can be used for loading
ammunition. BEML has developed the Field artillery tractor for gun towing applications involving 130mm/155mm
medium guns with accessories and ammunition. BEML has developed vehicles, which can lay bridges, carry radars and
build pontoon bridge systems for the defence forces. BEML has also developed aircraft towing tractors that find
applications at aerodromes for towing aircraft. Other vehicles manufactured by BEML include the armoured recovery
vehicle that has been developed in collaboration with Burma, Poland and are deployed in wartime operations/forward
areas to salvage damaged tanks. BEML has also indigenously developed aircraft weapon loading equipment for lifting
and positioning weapons, missiles, fuel tanks and aviation components onto the wings and fuselage of fighter aircraft.
The Committee was informed that BEML is backed by world class R&D and state of the art technology from global
partners like Bucyrus, Komatsu, Tatra, Voest Alpine, IGM and Bumar labedy and this has enabled BEML to achieve
high standards in product engineering and gain international competence.
 
4.17.2  The Committee was apprised of BEML’s strength in the area of railway equipment like broad-gauge rail
coaches, day coaches, parcel vans, luggage cum brake vans. BEML has a dedicated facility to produce integral rail
coaches and other railway-related equipment. BEML has also taken up manufacture of electric-multiple units heralding
its entry into intra –city urban rapid transport system.
 
4.17.3  The Committee was informed that 60 percent of BEML’s annual sale of machines goes into coal and mining
sectors. Railway and Defence sectors  add up to 10 percent of the sales. The rest constitutes users like electricity boards,
port trusts, cement companies, irrigation/construction projects and private contractors. When asked about the efforts
been made by BEML to enter the export route the committee was informed that BEML has been recognized as a star
export house and has been exporting to over 30 countries. The committee also enquired into the efforts being taken by
BEML for cost reduction. The CMD informed that BEML is now adopting an integrated manufacturing programme
including on-line decision making to reduce the time and cost factor. He also informed that the marketing operations
nationwide are connected by wide-area network to a central database at Head quarters, enabling the company to stay
closer to users and also provide the management with authentic feedback.
 
4.17.4  The CMD apprised the Committee that BEML has not been getting adequate cooperation from the Ministry of
Railways as far as placing of work orders for its railway coach manufacturing facility is concerned resulting in a huge
non utilization of the facility rendering a large number of employees idle.
OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS
 
4.18.1  The Committee was pleased to note that BEML had been showing profits since its inception. However, the
Committee was concerned to note that there has been a constant decline in the profits over the past several years. The
Committee feels that BEML has not made adequate efforts to expand its market base. The Committee recommends that
BEML should resort to aggressive marketing and explore new areas beyond their traditional customers to expand their

82nd Report

market base. In this context the Committee feels that BEML should develop value added products so as to garner a
larger share of the market. The Committee is of the view that with the infrastructure sector looking up there are
tremendous opportunities for BEML. The Committee also feels that BEML should also explore the possibilities of
providing maintenance service for high cost machines.
 
4.18.2  The Committee was deeply concerned to note that BEML has not been able to get adequate work orders for its
railway coach-manufacturing unit at Bangalore. The Committee is of the opinion that BEML should approach
organizations like the Delhi metro corporation to obtain work orders, and the issue should be taken up with the Railway
authorities at the highest level.
 
4.18.3  The Committee also observed that having regard to the vital sector in which the unit is operating the structure of
the MOU should be more appropriately geared to this factor.  It was observed the focus on financial performance, which
is being reiterated in the MOU, should be altered to shift the focus on more important factors of national interest. Hence
the MOU should accord higher weightage to performance parameters relating R&D, contribution to defense, product
development for difficult terrains like high altitude movement vehicles, movement vehicles for areas like Rann of Kutch
etc.
 
4.18.4  This apart, the Committee felt that since the MOU is a mutually agreed document on performance parameters, a
focus shift in the contribution of Government for this type of PSE is also imperative.  The performance parameters of
the Department of Defense Production and Supply in the MOU should lay emphasis on more tangible factors like
facilitating more orders from Railways for their products, export promotion for their remote controlled armoured
vehicles, extension of use of export offices of other PSUs like Bharat Electronics etc in other countries for promotion of
BEML products etc.
 
4.18.5  The committee also felt that MOUs should contain weightage for energy efficiency and resource efficiency
efforts as they also are to liable to reflect in the Balance Sheet of the Company under the Companies Act.
 
4.18.6  The Committee also felt that since the unit is operating in a strategic sector it is imperative that it has a sound
policy for retention and upgradation of skills of its Human Resource.  This is more than imperative for an unit like
BEML having regard to its strategic contribution to India’s defence and infrastructure sector. It is, therefore, felt that the
weightage for HRD should also be higher.
 (V)      HINDUSTAN AERONAUTICS LIMITED
 
5.1       Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL), was established in 1940 at Bangalore by a Private Entrepreneur – Shri
Walchand Hirachand as Hindustan Aircraft (Pvt.) Limited. In 1945, it was taken over by Government of India and

under licence from the then USSR. Hindustan Aircraft Limited and Aeronautics India Limited (AIL) were merged to
form Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) on 1
st October, 1964. HAL is the largest Defence Public Sector Unit and is
an MoU Company and has been declared as a “Mini Ratna”, Category-1 Company. HAL’s major customers are, Indian
Air Force, Indian Navy, Indian Coast Guard, Border Security Force and Department of Space. A Board, consisting of

5.2       The company has produced over 3,400 aircraft and 3,100 engines and has indigenously taken care of the

time ALH to IAF, Navy and Coast Guard during March, 2002. HAL has also designed and developed low cost Light

handling, Anti-Smuggling Roles. The first batch of Lancer was supplied to Indian Army during the year 2000-01. HAL
is a major participant in the Light Combat Aircraft (LCA) programme. The company has launched the Design and
Development of Intermediate Jet Trainer (IJT) Programme. This will provide cost effective solution for training needs

customer but HAL was now trying to enter the international market through the export route. In this context HAL has
begun making components for several international aircraft manufacturers and has also begun servicing of aircrafts.

imports only in cases where indigenous production is not possible. Besides Government should also provide incentive

VI.       NUCLEAR POWER CORPORATION OF INDIA LTD.
 
            Nuclear Power Corporation of India Ltd. (NPCIL) is a public sector enterprise under the Department of Atomic
Energy (DAE), Government of India. It was registered on 17 September 1987 with the objective of operating the atomic
power stations and implementing the atomic power projects for generation of electricity in pursuance with the schemes
and programmes of the GOI under atomic energy act 1962.
 
6.1       Background Prior To Formation of NPCIL

Prior to the formation of NPCIL, the design, construction and operation of the nuclear power plants were carried out as
a departmental activity under DAE. In 1967, Power Projects Engineering Division (PPED), a unit of DAE,  was formed
with the responsibility of design, construction and operation  of the Nuclear Power Plants. PPED was converted into
Nuclear Power Board (NPB) in the year 1984 which was again a governmental unit of DAB with increased delegation
of  powers to the unit. In September 1987, NPB was converted into NPCIL and the assets of  NPB  except the first unit
of Rajasthan Atomic Power Station (RAPS-l ) were transferred to NPCIL.
 
6.2       Authorized Share Capital
 
The authorised share capital of the company is Rs. 100,000 million, of  which Rs.63,826.70 million is paid up as on
March 31, 2002 and is fully subscribed by the Government of India.
 
6.3       Major Activities of NPCIL
 
6.3.1    The main activities of the company are design construction, commissioning and operation of nuclear power
plants. The company is operating six nuclear power stations with 14 units and is implementing, construction of four
ongoing nuclear power projects. The existing operating power stations of the Company are Tarapur Atomic Power
Station Units-l&2 (TAPS-l&2-2X160 MWe) Maharashtra, Rajasthan Atomic Power Station Unit-2 to 4 (RAPS-2-, 3&4-
lX200 + 2X220 MWe), Madras Atomic Power Station Units-1 &2 (MAPS-1&2- 2X170 MWe) Tamil Nadu, Narora
Atomic Power Station Units-l &2 ( NAPS-1&2-2X220 MWe) UP, Kakrapar Atomic Station LTnits-l&2 (IT..APS-l&2-
2X220 MWe) Gujarat and Kaiga Atomic Power station (Kaiga-l&2- 2X220 MWe),  Karnataka  RAPS-l- 100 MWe
Rajasthan is managed by  NPCIL on behalf of DAE.   The aggregate nuclear capacity  in operation in the country,
including RAPS-1, is 2720 MWe.
 
6.3.2    The projects currently under execution are 2X54O  MWe PHWRs  at Tarapur, Maharashtra (TAPP-3&4), 2X220
MWe PHWRs at   Kaiga, Karnataka,   2X220 MWe PHWRs at Rawatbhata, Rajasthan and  2X1000 MWe  VVERs  at
Kudankulam, Tamilnadu   (KK-1&2) .  The  project at Kudankulam is being set up in  co-operation with Russian
Federation.
 
6.4       Development Phase of Nuclear Power in India
 
6.4.1    The basic research in the nuclear field commenced about four decades ago in units of DAE. The initial R&D and
the experience in setting up and operations of  research reactors provided the core competence for the nuclear power
programme.  DAE, the Administrative Ministry, has  established over the years  comprehensive .capability in the entire
spectrum of nuclear fuel cycle in terms of fuel, special materials for nuclear power plants and nuclear waste
management facilities etc.
 
6.4.2    NPCIL has acquired comprehensive capability for designing, constructing, commissioning and operating nuclear
power plants. PHWRs of 220 MWe -unit size developed indigenously have reached a significant level of maturity.
Development of 540 MWe PIIWR has also been carried out indigenously and the  first  two  units are being set up at
Tarapur (TAPP-3&4). The 540 MWe unit rating of PHWR.s is also being updated to about 680 MWe with minimal
design changes and partial , boiling in the coolant channels for setting up PHWRs beyond TAPP-3&4.
 
6.4.3    The path of self- reliance has been chosen from the very beginning of the programme. Cost of generation from
nuclear power plants is comparable to contemporary coal thermal power plants located away from coal-mines. Nuclear
power is also associated with the advantage of being devoid of carbon-dioxide releases. The indigenous industries have
gained intense experience and are now in a position to take up the manufacture of critical nuclear components with high
precision.
 
With this background, nuclear power programme is now poised for rapid growth.
 
6.5       Potential of Nuclear Energy in India
 
6.5.1    With the approach of three-stage nuclear power progrmnme of DAE with pressurized heavy water reactors

(PHWRs) using natural uranium in the first stage, fast breeder reactors (FBRs) in the second stage and reactors using
U233 in thorium-U233 cycle in the third stage, the potential for electricity generation in the long-term is significant.
India's uranium resources are modest, but thorium resources are large, and the three-stage programme as above  will
enable utilising the full energy potential of uranium by  recycling pollution in the  second stage and ultimately utilize
thorium in third stage for electricity generation. The first stage programme of PHWRs with 220 ~1Vle and 540 MWe

6.5.2    The Indira Gandhi1Center  for Atomic Research of DAE has embarked  upon  design of 500 MWe protype  
Fast  Breeder Reactor (PFBR) .  Construction of PFBR is  planned  to commence in X Plan.  PFBR being prototype 
commercial scale fast reactor,   will be front   runner of FBR  technology.
 
6.5.3    An Advanced Heavy water Reactor (AHWR), as technology demonstrator   for large-scale  utilisation of thorium
for power production, is also planned for commencement of  construction in the X plan by BARC.
 
6.6     Safety & Environmental Protection
 
6.6.1    NPCIL accords the highest priority on Quality Assurance (QA) and safety and environmental protection at all
stages of the nuclear power programme. The Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) which is an independent and
statutory body in terms of the Atomic Energy Act 1962, monitors, prescribes and enforces safety review at NPCIL.
Well-known design safety principles like defence-in-depth, multiple barriers, release of radioactivity and fail safe
designs are adopted in the engineering of the plants so that  releases from the plants will be well within the prescribed
limits stipulated by AERB.
 
 
During safety review at operational stage, release from the plants are monitored and regulated to be within the stipulated
limits. Environment Survey Laboratories are set up at each operating nuclear power station, which monitor a number of
samples of air, water, road and other products in the environment around the power station for radioactivity and the
reports of these laboratories are reviewed by AERB. Nuclear power is one of the environmentally clean sources for bulk
generation of electricity. It is very relevant in protection of the environment from greenhouse gases, acid rain and smog.
6.7          Human Resource Development
 
Human resource development has been given the required priority from the  early stages of nuclear power development
consistent with knowledge, expertise  and skill   required for setting up and operating the nuclear power stations. 
Specialised training units like BARC Training School and NPCIl Nuclear Training Centre and well designed
programmes like in-plant induction training, qualification of operation staff to different positions as per requirements of
AERB, on the job training and training in specific specialised in the human resource development in NPCIL.

            NPCIL is taking action on all fronts to complete the above tasks

6.11     HISTORY OF MOU SYSTEM IN NPCL
 
6.11.1    The company, after its formation in September, 1987 studied the MOU system which a few Public Sector
Enterprises (PSEs) had adopted them,.  Seeing the advantages of the system for performance  improvement of the
company, NPCIL   for the first time entered into MOU with the Administrative Ministry i.e. Department of Atomic
Energy for the year 1991-92.  Since then, every year, MOU has been  signed between NPCIL and DAE.   The
performance evaluation is carried out based   on the stated commitments in the MOU.
 
6.11.2     The process of arriving at MOU is as follows:
 
(i)         Compiling comprehensive set of criteria for company’s performance evaluation.  These criteria broadly cover
the Generating Performance, profitability, Project milestones, quality assurance, Human Resource Development,
Research & Development, Environment Protection & Public Awareness, etc.  This   fulfills one of the objectives of the
industrial policy resolution of  1956 that the performance of all PSE’s should be judged by their over-all results.
 
(ii)        NPCIL assigns weightages to different criteria of the MOU based on the relative importance of the indicators
and priorities between different objectives of the company.The aspects stated above are evolved through a process of
participation by respective functional Directorates. The target values for, each parameter are fixed, based on the
commitment of executing agencies. The process of involvement is complemented by other documents like performance
budget, annual plan or capital budget and revenue budget generated by the company. After in-house deliberations and
finalisation, the details are reviewed at DAE, before the MOU is proposed for consideration of DPE. The institutional
arrangement for MOU facilitates the third party vetting by Department of Public Enterprises (DPE). The industry
specific Adhoc Task Force (ATF) of DPE vigorously examines the MOU and gives clearance for entering into
performance contract of MOU of NPCIL and DAE.

6.12     DISCUSSIONS WITH THE MANAGEMENT OF NPCIL
 
6.12.1    Shri V.K. Sharma, the acting CMD of NPCIL, made a presentation on the history of the corporation since its
incorporation in 1987 till today, including its ongoing projects and thereafter, the Committee deliberated with officers of
the NPCIL and the following points emanated from the discussions.
 
6.12.2   Since 1987 additional capacity of 1760 MWE has been created through commencement of commercial
operation at NAPS-1&2, KAPS and kaiga
 
6.12.3    The present Nuclear power capacity in the country is 2720 Mwe and projection for enhancement of this
capacity is 6680 Mwe by 2008 in the light of additional capacity enhancement of 3960 Mwe through completion of
ongoing projects at TAPP, KAIga and Rapp and Kudankulam. Overall contribution of Nuclear energy in the total
energy component of the country being a meagre three percent it was informed that Nuclear energy is highly cost
intensive and it has also to be seen in the context of energy contribution growing in other traditional sector through
capacity creation. Nuclear energy generation involves higher iterative process due to high order risk to ensure reduction
of occurrence of risk or to ensure improbability of occurrence of risk.  Incidentally the Nuclear power sector in the
country has zero accident record since 1968. In addition, availability of raw material uranium of 238 category is scarce
and India has deposits of U235 only and conversion of U 235 to 238 is also a cost intensive process.
 
6.12.4    The committee also sought an assurance against occurrence of a Chernobyl type accidents.  In this context, the
Committee was reassured that Chernobyl type technology is not licensable, and the NPCIL follows an extremely
transparent policy besides, having a sound system of in built periodic safety audits and stock taking.
 
6.12.5   In addition, the NPCIL is also learning from accidents in other countries.Moreover, as a member of IAEC India
is bound by their safety and other provision of Nuclear Power use and hence accidents are near improbable.
 
6.12.6    The Committee was also informed that the capacity utilization is about 87 percent  and there is a continuous
improvement of capacity factors.
           
6.12.7   The Committee was informed that one of the reasons for the slow growth of nuclear power in our country has
been the indigenous technology development phase that the nuclear power programme had to go through. Nuclear
power plants are very complex and require millions of smaller and bigger items/components to be designed, fabricated
and assembled. The licensing of nuclear power plants involves a complex regulatory process in which all the safety
aspects are checked. The nuclear power plants have been installed in advanced countries by sharing of technology
developed by different countries and using their fabrication capabilities. On account of the restrictive trade barriers and
technology denial regime prevalent for India, all the development had to be done within the country and this took time
initially.
 
6.12.8     The Committee was also apprised that Nuclear power has no significant avenues for overseas financing. It has
to rely on Government budgetary support in combination with domestic borrowing and internal surplus. A programme
of setting up of 10,000 MWe of nuclear power capacity by 2000 was formulated. There were problems on the
availability of financial resources during the VIII Five-Year Plan. Therefore, this programme could not be implemented
as envisaged.

policy for retention and upgradation of skills of its Human Resource.  This is more than imperative for an unit like HAL
having regard to its strategic contribution to India’s defence and infrastructure sector. It is thereore felt that the
weightage for HRD should also be higher.
(5.8.5)
 
            Also, higher weightage should be accorded in the MOU for safety parameters besides, developing fail-safe
technologies in the helicopter developmental area.
(5.8.6)
 
            In the context, of the fact that India is importing advance jet trainers the Committee sought to know why HAL
cannot develop these advance jet trainers.  It was observed by the Committee that there is requirement of sufficient lead
time with continuous and adequate support for taking up such projects, and hence the committee felt that it was
imperative for the Government to not only extend continuous and adequate support, but also ensure a participation in the
for HAL in the defence demand and technology forecasting endeavors.
(5.8.7)
 
            The Committee was concerned to note that several equipments, which could have been indigenously developed
with the expertise of HAL, were imported at substantial costs. The Committee recommends preference to HAL to
manufacture all such components/equipments should be given.
(5.8.8)
              The Committee was pleased to note that NPCIL had been performing extremely well since its inception.
(6.13.1)
 
   The Committee also observed that having regard to the vital sector in which the unit is operating the structure of the
MOU should be more appropriately geared to this factor.  It was observed the focus on financial performance being
iterated in the MOU should be altered to shift the focus on more important factors of national interest. Hence the MoU
should accord higher weightage to performance parameters relating R&D, contribution to defense, contribution to
Indian Space Research Programme, Disaster Management and Relief efforts.
(6.13.2)
 
The Committee felt R&D, especially in the areas of import substitution in terms of development of new materials as
well as new process technologies, should be accorded much higher weightage in the interest of impetus to Indian
Nuclear Programmes.
(6.13.3)
  
This apart, the Committee felt that since the MOU is a mutually agreed document on performance parameters, a focus

Department of Atomic Energy in the MOU should emphasis on more tangible factors like facilitating more in enabling
the company in recovering dues from SEB. 
(6.13.4)
 
The Committee also felt that MOUs should contain weightage for energy efficiency and resource efficiency efforts as
they also are to liable to reflect in the Balance Sheet of the Company under the Companies Act.
(6.13.5)
The Committee also felt that since the unit is operating in a strategic sector, it is imperative that it has a sound policy for
retention and upgradation of skills of its Human Resource.  This is more than imperative for a unit like NPCIL having
regard to its strategic contribution to India’s defence and infrastructure sector. It is therefore felt that the weightage for
HRD should also be higher.  At the same time the excellent expertise and human resource base should also be exported
in the form participation in safety audit teams constituted by IAEC, mutual inspection teams etc
(6.13.6)
            Also higher weightage should be accorded in the MOU for safety parameters besides, developing fail safe

 Ecological and environmentally sustainable operation is also a vital area of concern for Nuclear Power.  Weightage to

            As regards introduction of systems upgradation like Extra Resource Planning etc, the Committee observed that
the NPCIL is having its own LAN systems and felt little need for a performance enhancing systems application like

needs to be alert to organizational decays and take remedial measures through process reengineering of its work
systems. Hence, MOU weight should also be accorded for this appropriately.
(6.13.9)
 
            The Committee feels that considering the self-reliant manner in which nuclear power has been developed,
Government should provide higher financial allocation and resources for the growth of Nuclear power.

         The Sub-Committee IV for Ministry fo r Agro and Rural Industries at its meeting held on 14 th  
March and 41h April 2002 decided to  study the implementation of Pr ime Minister Rozgar Yojana
(PMRY in the States of Andhra Pr adesh, Karnataka and Kerala. The Sub-Committee visited the States 
of Andhra Pradesh Karnataka and Kerala from 201h to  271h June 2002 and held discussions with the 
officials of  Ministry of Agro & Rural Industries, Stat e Government and Banks on issues pertaining to
PMRY. 
  
PMRY - AN OVERVIEW OF THE SCHEME 
  
1.1    The Prime Minister's Rozgar Yojana was launched on 2nd Oct ober, 1993 with a view to providing
self-employment opportunities to educated unemplo yed youth in the country. The scheme was made 
operational with effect from Is t April, 1994. Prime Minister's Rozgar Yojanawas launched on 2nd
October, 1993. The scheme was designed to provide employment to more than  a million persons by
setting up seven lakh micro enterp rises during the Eight Five Year  Plan (1993-97), through industry, 
services and business routes. The scheme was operated in urban ar eas only during 1993-94, and in both 
urban and rural areas of the country from 1994-95 onwards. From 1994-95 the erstwhile-Self-
Employment Scheme for the Educat ed Unemployed Youth (SEEUY) was merged into PMRY. During
the Eight Plan a total of 7.75 lakh cases were sancti oned and out of these, lo ans were reported to have
been disbursed in 6.52 lakh cases as reported by the Reserve Bank of In dia (REI). Until now, nearly 15
educated unemployed youth have benefited from th e scheme. The PMRY is continuing in the Tenth
Plan period.

a total of 2.63 lakh cases were sa nctioned and in 2.09 lakh cases loan s were disbursed. During 1998-99,

cases loans were disbursed as per the available reports from REI. Furt her, to enhance the coverage and
scope of the PMRY scheme, it has been modified si nce 1st April, 1999. The modified salient features o

1.3    The target envisaged for 1999-2000 was 2.20 lakh beneficiaries. Against this target, 1,14,587 cases 
have been sanctioned, and disbursement took plac e in 59,845 cases as reporte d upto the month ending
December, 1999. The Target for 2002-03 remains at the level of Rs.2.20 lakhs, as was the case on 2001-
02. 
  
1.4    The Committee observes that the target (2.20 lakh beneficiaries) set for PMRY is too low to have
any significant impact on the creati on of employment opportunities in the country. This issue weighted
on the Committee's discussion with of ficials of State Government, Mini stry of Agro & Rural Industries
during its visit to Andhra Pradesh, Kamataka, Kerala. The Committee no ted that the target fixed each
year for PMRY has remained st atic during the last three year s i.e. for 2000-01, 2001-02 and 2002-03 
only 2.20 lakh persons were to be c overed under PMRY scheme. This figure, when divided between the
states and thereafter, among districts of each state, is like a drop. Th is figure is too minuscule to have
any noticeable impact on the unemployment scenario in a country of millions. 
  
1.5    The Ministry of Small Scale Industries, with whom the matter was taken up explained that the 
fixing of target was based on two aspects: - 
(a)
    Basic Target which is fixed, and is based on th e State's population as in 1991. This target is 
given by the Planning Commissi on, and is based on the employm ent potential and the numbe r
of unemployed registered with Employment Excha nge. An annual. target of 2.2 lakhs is given
for 2002-03, on an all India basis. This is communicated in March every year, for the next year.
(b)   Additional Target: This is vari able and is fixed on the basis of recovery position during the
previous year, and the performance in the previous year. This is communicated during May. 
         The Committee was also informed that th ere is a Government of Indi a guideline that 125 per cent
of target must also be achieved. 
  
1.6    However, the Committee was of the view that  the overall target for PM RY should be increased so
that states could be given enhanc ed targets, and more and more people can be brought under the ambit
of the scheme each year.
